magic-the-gathering.context_blurb: Magic: the Gathering is a trading card game — the very first one ever made — launched in August 1993 by a tiny company based in Renton, Washington, right across the lake from Seattle. Each player builds a custom deck from a huge pool of cards and duels another player by casting spells, summoning creatures, and paying the mana (magical energy) that lands produce, trying to reduce the opponent's twenty life points to zero. The game runs on five colors of mana, each with its own personality and tricks, and dozens of expansion sets have been printed over the decades. The earliest print runs from 1993 and 1994 are now treasured by collectors, with single rare cards from the first run selling for the price of a sports car. Magic kicked off the whole collectible-card craze that later swept up Pokemon and Yu-Gi-Oh!, and it remains the gold standard against which every later card game is measured. The lore around its early tournaments, misprints, and banned cards is a world unto itself, and the hobby's grognards remember the mid-1990s the way old wargamers remember the first boxes of Dungeons & Dragons. Many of its original designers and promoters came out of the Pacific Northwest's board-game and role-playing scene, and the stories of its first few years are legend among players.

pro-wrestling-wwf-wwe.context_blurb: Professional wrestling is scripted combat theater performed as a live athletic spectacle, and from the mid-1980s through the early 2000s the industry was ruled by two American companies: Vince McMahon's World Wrestling Federation (WWF, later renamed WWE) based in Connecticut, and Ted Turner's rival Atlanta-based World Championship Wrestling (WCW). The two companies fought a brutal ratings war on Monday nights in the 1990s, now remembered as the Monday Night Wars, trading champions, storylines, and famous match endings in a desperate scramble to keep fans. The era produced wrestling's biggest icons — larger-than-life characters who became household names, each with their own entrance music, catchphrase, costume, and signature finishing move. The companies ran a yearly calendar of huge pay-per-view spectacles, including the spring super-show that became the single biggest annual event in the whole industry, and the summer and winter stadium tours that ran alongside it. The infamous 1997 Montreal Screwjob incident is still argued about by fans today. Wrestling fans treat the specific finishing moves, catchphrases, and swerves of this period as sacred canon, and the Attitude Era in particular (roughly 1997-2002) is remembered as the medium's wildest, boldest commercial peak. Classic wrestling trivia almost always rewards someone who grew up watching cable TV at the right time. If you are curious about the medium, the real gateway is any of the big pay-per-views of the 1980s or the 1990s Monday Night Raw and Nitro episodes — they are the shows the whole industry's style was built on.

seattle-seahawks.context_blurb: The Seattle Seahawks are Seattle's National Football League (NFL) franchise, founded as a 1976 expansion team and based in Seattle, Washington. They play their home games indoors at Lumen Field (previously CenturyLink Field and Qwest Field) wearing navy, action green, and silver. For most of their history the franchise was middling, but a run of early-2010s teams built by their head coach of that era turned the team into a powerhouse — appearing in two Super Bowls back to back and famously winning Super Bowl XLVIII against the Denver Broncos in February 2014. That era's defense was so punishing that it earned its own fan nickname, and the team's star running back and quarterback both became household names. The franchise has given American football some of its loudest home-field advantages (crowd noise once registered as a small earthquake), one of its greatest wide receivers in the franchise's early years, and one of its most-second-guessed Super Bowl play calls. The players, coaches, Super Bowl moments, and Kingdome-era history are all part of the shared vocabulary of being a Pacific Northwest kid. For a Seattle sports fan, learning the two Super Bowl runs is a rite of passage, and old game footage of the playoff wins against the 49ers and the Saints is on YouTube and worth hunting down.

seattle-mariners.context_blurb: The Seattle Mariners are a Major League Baseball (MLB) team in the American League, founded as a 1977 expansion franchise and based in Seattle, Washington. They played their first decades indoors at the concrete Kingdome before moving in 1999 to the open-air Safeco Field (now T-Mobile Park). The 1990s and early 2000s were the franchise's golden age — a left-handed slugging center fielder with a gorgeous swing, a Japanese right fielder who revolutionized hitting after crossing the Pacific in 2001, a towering left-handed strikeout pitcher, and the beloved designated hitter whose number became a street name in Seattle. The 2001 Mariners tied an MLB record by winning 116 regular-season games, and the 1995 team gave the city one of the most legendary playoff moments in franchise history — a famous eleventh-inning hit scored from first base. The Mariners also hold a less happy record: the longest active postseason drought in North American pro sports stretched for most of the 2000s and 2010s. The catching tandem of father-and-son outfielders in 1990, perfect games, and the Kingdome-to-Safeco-to-T-Mobile transition are all part of the fabric of Mariners fandom. For a Seattle sports fan, the archive highlight reels of Griffey robbing home runs over the center-field wall and Ichiro's cannon arm from right field are both worth hunting down on YouTube — they capture something no written stat line can.

anime-dragon-ball.context_blurb:
Akira Toriyama started Dragon Ball in Weekly Shonen Jump in 1984: a boy alone in the mountains, black hair in spikes, a monkey tail, a red-tipped power pole, holding an orange ball with four stars in it that his late Grandpa Gohan left him, and the series named for those balls is Dragon Ball. The boy is Son Goku. Toriyama built him from Sun Wukong of Journey to the West, which is where the tail, staff and surname come from. His previous comic, a 1980 gag series about a robot girl called Arale built by a bumbling inventor in Penguin Village, is Dr. Slump.

A blue-haired teenager arrives on a motorbike with a radar that pings near the orbs, and she is Bulma. Her father founded Capsule Corp; Toriyama named the family after underwear. Holding all seven balls is not sufficient by itself, because the wish needs calling the dragon Shenron by name with all seven balls together. Afterwards they scatter and go inert for a year.

Being a Saiyan has consequences. Under a full moon Goku's tail turns him into a giant ape called the Oozaru, hundreds of feet tall, ten times stronger and almost mindless. Dragon Ball Z opens with his brother Raditz, and the old enemy turned ally who fires his Special Beam Cannon through both brothers while Goku holds Raditz in place, dying with them, is Piccolo.

Namek is where the series became what people remember. The tyrant Frieza kills Goku's oldest friend, the short bald monk Krillin, in front of him, and what detonates Goku's rage is Frieza killing Krillin in front of him. His hair goes gold and his eyes green in a form unseen for a thousand years, the Super Saiyan. The manga gives the planet five minutes to live; the anime, waiting on Toriyama's pages, stretched that into roughly 19 episodes, spread across about half a year of weekly broadcast.

Then Dr. Gero's bio-android arrives, built from the cells of every fighter, needing two earlier models to reach his perfect form, and the two he hunts are Androids 17 and 18, the twin siblings. A teenaged Trunks had already come back from a future in which Goku died of a heart virus, carrying a specific anti-heart-virus pharmaceutical from the future, in a Capsule Corp medicine bottle. Father and son train for the fight in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber above Korin Tower, where a day is a year and trainees get two cumulative days (two years of training) total per person across their lifetime. At the Cell Games Goku steps aside and sends his son in, because Goku has determined Gohan has greater untapped potential and a hidden form Cell hasn't seen. When Cell crushes Android 16 mid-sentence, Gohan ascends to Super Saiyan 2.

The Buu saga keeps the jokes running. The world champion who claims Gohan's victory for himself is a parody of a bombastic Western pro wrestler, with a name riffing on Hulk Hogan. Fat Buu befriends him and his dog, and the dog is Bee. The champion then redeems himself by talking the whole planet into raising its arms for Goku's borrowed-energy attack, The Spirit Bomb (Genki Dama).

Two production stories matter. Toriyama's editor Kazuhiko Torishima took to the Super Saiyan idea at once and let it through with almost no editorial changes. And the anime-only Red Ribbon detour had already produced a classic Toriyama trick, in which the cat sage at the top of Korin Tower makes Goku strong by promising him The Sacred Water, which turns out to have been a Karin Tower trick to make Goku train.

On television, Toei's 1986 opening was Makafushigi Adventure!, and the 1989 Z theme sung by Hironobu Kageyama is Cha-La Head-Cha-La. Toei rebuilt the show for its twentieth anniversary as Kai, cutting 291 episodes to about 167, and the work was Toei Animation in-house, with new dubbing and a re-edit by Kazuhiro Furuhashi. In English, one Funimation actor carried Vegeta, Piccolo, Yamcha and Master Roshi at once, and he is Christopher Sabat. Goku reached English first through the 1996 Ocean dub in Canada, where Ian Corlett began the role and Peter Kelamis took it over partway through, before Sean Schemmel won it in 1999. Vegeta's scouter reads over eight thousand in the Japanese, and the nine-thousand version everybody quotes came in with the English dub, so the real reading is Eight thousand. Dragon Ball GT, having no manga to follow, invented a red-furred form called Super Saiyan 4.

studio-ghibli.context_blurb: Studio Ghibli is a Japanese hand-drawn animation studio in Tokyo, founded in 1985 by two directors and their producer-partner after the success of a 1984 pre-Ghibli film about a wind-valley princess in a poisoned future world. The studio became famous worldwide for warm watercolor backgrounds, slow quiet pacing, flying scenes, impossibly detailed food, and stories centered on strong young girls encountering spirits, witches, forest gods, and talking animals. The studio's co-founding director directed the beloved films about two sisters finding a woodland spirit in rural Japan, a thirteen-year-old witch delivering packages in a European-styled town, a bathhouse of spirits in a hidden world, a wolf-raised girl and a cursed prince, and a wizard's walking castle. His quieter co-founder directed the heartbreaking wartime story of a brother and sister in 1945 Kobe and the reflective films that filled the studio's other half. Ghibli guards its hand-drawn style fiercely and has long resisted computer animation, and the studio became the gold standard against which almost every other animated feature is measured. In 1996 the studio signed a worldwide distribution deal with Disney, and Ghibli's films became permanent library titles in American and European homes. If you have never seen a Ghibli film, the easiest starting point is the gentle 1988 countryside story about two sisters — it is widely considered the perfect introduction to the whole studio's style.

neon-genesis-evangelion.context_blurb: Neon Genesis Evangelion is a 1995 Japanese anime series directed by Hideaki Anno at Studio Gainax, set in a near-future Tokyo under attack by huge geometric monsters called Angels that only three traumatized teenage pilots strapped inside towering biomechanical robots can stop. The show is set after a mysterious cataclysm called the Second Impact wiped out much of the world's population, and the surviving world is run by a shadowy UN-backed organization headquartered deep underground. What began as a mecha-robot action show gradually peeled away into one of the most psychologically unsettling anime ever made — the teenage pilots are depressed and lonely, the series is loaded with Jewish and Christian mythology used as striking visuals, and the famously bizarre ending split the plot action from the pilots' inner thoughts drawn in half-finished pencil sketches. Evangelion's merchandise and designs, especially the pale blue-haired pilot Rei Ayanami and the red-plug-suited Asuka, defined an entire era of Japanese pop culture and remain instantly recognizable decades later. The studio Gainax was founded by college-aged science-fiction fans who had broken through at a 1981 convention opening-ceremony short, and Evangelion was their all-in bet — Anno famously said he poured his own real depression into every frame of the show.

cowboy-bebop.context_blurb:
Cowboy Bebop is twenty-six episodes made at Sunrise in 1998 and directed by Shinichiro Watanabe, about bounty hunters working the solar system in 2071 out of a battered ship called the Bebop. Watanabe's pitch named two American genres of the mid-century as the show's parents, film noir and the western, and the show is exactly that, since a bounty board is a western device while the lighting and the fatalism are noir. Spike himself is built out of Bruce Lee and 1970s Hong Kong cinema.

The crew is a lanky former syndicate hitman called Spike, a gruff ex-policeman named Jet with a prosthetic arm, the con-woman Faye, a barefoot child hacker called Edward, and a dog. The dog is a data dog, a genetically enhanced Pembroke Welsh corgi cleverer than most of the humans, and his name is Ein. The creators kept Ed's gender deliberately hard to read through voice and clothes and manner, and what they have said about the character is that Ed is Female, but with androgynous presentation.

The music is why people who do not watch anime watch this. Yoko Kanno wrote around eighty pieces for the run and fronts the studio band that plays them, a band named for the thing drivers are told to put on, The Seatbelts. The opening is a big-band blast with its title flashing up in one word, Tank! A walking bass drives it, the melody belongs to the tenor saxophone, and the horns are arranged to clash cheerfully with a cyberpunk future. Mai Yamane sang many of the vocal tracks.

The credits look as deliberate as they sound. The design borrows from the mid-century American title designer who made the sequences for Hitchcock, Preminger and Kubrick, and the trick is Saul Bass-inspired silhouetted figures against blocks of solid color, with hand-typeset character cards.

Spike's past is the thread under the comedy. He belonged to an elite unit of a crime organisation called the Red Dragon Syndicate and faked his death to get out, and the colleague from that unit who comes back for him is Vicious. His left eye is an implant from that old life, and he jokes that one eye sees the present and one sees the past; no single episode is built around how he lost it, and the episode fans point to is Episode 17, Mushroom Samba — though the eye is briefly referenced in the Ballad of Fallen Angels flashback. The two closing episodes borrow their title from a blues song, and the last of them is The Real Folk Blues, Part 2.

Getting the whole thing onto television took two tries. TV Tokyo found the violence and the tone too much and aired only half the run in 1998, and the full twenty-six went out uncut on the satellite channel WOWOW from October 1998 to April 1999. WOWOW did the same service for other adult anime of the period, and in 2001 Bebop crossed to America on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim, where for a great many viewers it was the first anime plainly made for grown-ups.

berserk.context_blurb:
Kentaro Miura published a Berserk prototype in 1988, began the serial in 1989, and drew it almost without a break until he died suddenly in May 2021, aged fifty-four, leaving one of the longest and most ferociously detailed epics anybody has attempted in comics. The world is a medieval Europe of mercenary bands, kings and demons. The hero is a huge scarred swordsman, branded for sacrifice and hunted by demons after dark, and his name is Guts. The sword he carries is a slab of iron almost as tall as he is, forged by the old blacksmith Godo for a king who wanted something a dragon could fall on, and it is called The Dragonslayer. Godo swore no human would ever swing it.

The spine of the series is a long flashback called the Golden Age, in which the young Guts fights for a rising mercenary army, the Band of the Hawk. Its commander is beautiful, golden-haired and set on owning a kingdom of his own one day, and he is Griffith. Casca, his second in command, loves him quietly. Miura spent volumes three to fourteen on this arc and treated it as the real story.

What ends the Golden Age is the Eclipse. Griffith, imprisoned, tortured and crippled, still carries a small red bead he has kept for years; it opens a portal, and the thing that opens it is The Behelit. On the other side wait the dark gods of the God Hand, who offer him rank in exchange for his whole company. When the Eclipse begins the God Hand numbers four, with Griffith being inducted as the fifth.

Every adaptation comes with an asterisk. Oriental Light and Magic made a twenty-five-episode television anime in 1997 that covered the Golden Age and stopped at the edge of the massacre, because the OVA was 25 episodes long but ended on a freeze-frame before the Eclipse to avoid graphic content for TV broadcast. Susumu Hirasawa's electronic-orchestral score, carried over from his work with the band P-Model, is famous in its own right, and the closing song is Waiting So Long. Studio 4C filmed the Eclipse in full across a trilogy in 2012 and 2013; a computer-animated series in 2016 tried to carry the story further and was never forgiven for how it looked.

Miura's last completed chapter was 364, in volume 41. His friend from high school Kouji Mori, who writes Holyland and says Miura told him the whole ending in detail, has carried the manga on since June 2022 with the assistants of Studio Gaga.

mobile-suit-gundam.context_blurb: Mobile Suit Gundam is a Japanese anime franchise created by director Yoshiyuki Tomino, launched in 1979 by Sunrise. It threw out the cartoon-style super-robot shows that had dominated 1970s Japanese TV and instead imagined giant piloted mechs — called mobile suits — as gritty military hardware, pulled on by sweating teenage soldiers in a sprawling war between Earth and the breakaway space colony state of Zeon. The original 1979 series flopped on first broadcast and was cut short by the network, but it exploded into a cultural phenomenon when Bandai released snap-together plastic kits — the famous Gunpla — letting kids build and paint the actual robots from the show. The franchise has run almost nonstop ever since, with new timelines, new wars, and dozens of spin-off series, films, and manga, including the 1995 series Gundam Wing that first conquered American TV through Cartoon Network's Toonami block, and the 2002 reboot Gundam SEED. Mobile Suit Gundam is treated by Japanese fans with reverence — the way American fans treat the original Star Wars trilogy. The original mobile-suit mechanical designs were drawn by Kunio Okawara, who essentially invented the visual grammar of serious anime mecha, and the franchise's models and model-kit lore are a whole hobby unto themselves.

akira.context_blurb:
Akira opens with a silent white blast erasing Tokyo in 1988 and then jumps thirty years forward into Neo-Tokyo, a neon megacity built on the crater, where bike gangs race through the streets and the army keeps psychic children in a laboratory. The man who wrote and drew the enormous manga it comes from directed the film as well, and he is Katsuhiro Otomo. His comic had been running in Young Magazine since 1982; he made the film halfway through it and changed the comic's ending afterwards.

The story turns on two friends. Tetsuo Shima crashes his bike, disappears into a military lab and comes back with powers nobody can hold; the leader of their gang, who spends the film chasing him through the city, is Kaneda. His red motorcycle is the most copied machine in animation.

Everything about the production was excessive for 1988. Otomo insisted the mouths be drawn to match voices already recorded, which reversed the usual order of work in anime, and more than 160,000 cels went into it, over twice the usual count. The money came from a consortium including Bandai, Kodansha and Toho, and the budget was approximately 11 million dollars, nearly double the previous record for Japanese animation. The jet-turbine howl of Kaneda's bike was never a jet at all, since it came from a modified Kawasaki Ninja motorcycle, recorded on a closed Tokyo street, and was then layered under drums.

The score is the other reason nobody forgets the film. Geinoh Yamashirogumi, an ensemble of university colleagues and amateur singers, recorded most of it before the animation existed, so the pictures were cut to fit the music, and the three sounds it was built from are taiko drums, Indonesian gamelan, and traditional Japanese noh chanting. The opening is one headlight in the dark, and then the title slams in on the drums.

Akira reached American cinemas on 25 December 1989 through Streamline Pictures, and for a generation of Western viewers it was the proof that animation could be serious and adult and frightening. Pioneer made a fresh English dub in 2001 with a new cast, Joshua Seth playing Tetsuo and Kaneda going to a voice actor familiar to anyone who watched Power Rangers: Johnny Yong Bosch. The sideways stop of the red bike has since been quoted in Ready Player One, in Chronicle, in Looper, in a Kanye West video and in the Spider-Verse sequel, so most people have seen the shot before they ever see the film.

ghost-in-the-shell.context_blurb:
Masamune Shirow began the Ghost in the Shell manga in 1989, and Production I.G made the film in 1995. The setting is a near-future megacity on a Hong Kong model where people have swapped more and more of the body for machinery and plug their brains straight into the network, which keeps the question of where a person stops and a machine starts permanently open. The Major, Motoko Kusanagi, is artificial from the neck down and human inside her skull, and she hunts the hacker known as the Puppet Master, who walks into other people's minds. The director of the film is Mamoru Oshii, who had made Patlabor before it.

Kusanagi is field commander of a small government counter-terror outfit under Chief Aramaki, with Batou as her second, and its name is among the most quoted designations in cyberpunk: Public Security Section 9.

The look of the thing changed the industry. For the famous fall from the skyscraper roof, and for the glowing data and the ghostly transparency, the studio put the traditional multi-plane camera together with a tool nobody had yet used this way in anime, which was computer graphics for compositing over hand-drawn cel animation. The Wachowskis showed the film to Joel Silver as the visual pitch for The Matrix, which is how much of the West met it second-hand.

rurouni-kenshin.context_blurb: Rurouni Kenshin is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Nobuhiro Watsuki from 1994 to 1999, with a popular 1996 anime from Studio Deen. It is set in Meiji-era Japan in the early 1870s, just after the samurai age officially ended and the country rushed into modernization. The main character is a wandering swordsman with a cross-shaped scar on his left cheek — a former imperial assassin from the civil war who has sworn never to kill again, and now carries a reverse-blade sword with its sharp edge facing himself. He takes up with a kind-hearted swordsmanship instructor at her Tokyo dojo and gets pulled into one government intrigue after another, meeting a cast of lively allies (a loudmouth brawler, a boy pickpocket, a woman doctor, a crafty swordsman-police captain) and tracking down former comrades-turned-villains from his assassin days. The anime adaptation ran into a common problem — the show caught up to the still-running manga — and Rurouni Kenshin has since generated several live-action film adaptations (starting in 2012) and manga sequels retelling the characters' later years. The Kyoto arc, following a scarred fire-wielding villain who plans to burn the new Meiji government to the ground, is widely considered the series' best.

trigun.context_blurb: Trigun is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yasuhiro Nightow, first serialized in 1995, and the 1998 anime adaptation directed by Satoshi Nishimura at Madhouse. It is set on a dusty desert planet with two suns, settled generations ago by human colonists whose arriving ships crash-landed, leaving them scattered in little frontier towns. The main character is a tall, spiky-blond, red-coat-wearing gunfighter with the biggest bounty on his head anyone has ever seen — he carries a long silver revolver and leaves wrecked frontier towns in his wake, though he insists he is actually a kind pacifist who never kills. He gets dogged across the desert by a pair of insurance-company agents trying to prevent any more property damage, and he eventually finds his cold, dark-coated brother and a terrifying order of assassins who serve him. The anime's dusty cowboy-planet aesthetic blends spaghetti-western visuals with science-fiction worldbuilding, and the manga continued in a later run called Trigun Maximum after Nightow moved to a new publisher. The main character's over-the-top gunslinger iconography is a love letter to the Spaghetti Western — right down to his revolver design, which is modeled on real 1800s cap-and-ball guns. If you love cowboy shows, Trigun is the best anime gateway there is — the hero's over-the-top gunslinger stance has launched a thousand fan drawings.

slayers.context_blurb: Slayers is a comedy fantasy Japanese light novel series by Hajime Kanzaka, launched in 1989, with a long-running manga adaptation and a 1995 anime from studio J.C.Staff. It stars a short, red-haired, bad-tempered teenage sorceress with the biggest ego and the biggest destructive spell in the setting, as she wanders a traditional sword-and-sorcery world picking fights with bandits, dragons, and dark lords, usually for the loot. She teams up with a dim-witted blond swordsman, a priestess-fighter, and a chimera experiment of a man whose body is permanently stitched together from several creatures, and the group argues their way through fantasy quests full of exploding villages and bad puns. The anime series was a huge hit on Japanese TV in the 1990s and crossed to the United States in the early 2000s, and the main character's voice actress Megumi Hayashibara became one of the most-heard voice actresses in all of anime — she also voices Rei Ayanami in Neon Genesis Evangelion and Faye Valentine in Cowboy Bebop. Slayers helped define the comedy-fantasy genre for a whole generation of later series. It is one of the great gateway anime for kids who love Dungeons & Dragons. If you are starting out in anime, Slayers' silly tone and classic fantasy world make it one of the all-time best introductions to the medium.

lupin-iii.context_blurb: Lupin III is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Monkey Punch (Kazuhiko Kato), first serialized in 1967, and a long-running anime franchise that has produced TV series, films, and specials almost nonstop from the 1970s to today. The main character is a wisecracking master thief in a bright-colored jacket and skinny tie, said to be the grandson of the gentleman thief Arsene Lupin from the classic early-1900s French novels by Maurice Leblanc. He steals the world's most impossible treasures with a crew of regulars — a sharpshooter in a fedora and gray suit, a stoic samurai swordsman who can cut anything, and a shifty femme-fatale whose loyalties change by the paycheck — while being chased all over the globe by a determined Interpol detective. The 1979 film The Castle of Cagliostro, directed by Hayao Miyazaki (right before he co-founded Studio Ghibli), is widely considered one of the best in the franchise and features one of the most-copied animated car chases ever made — Steven Spielberg has reportedly called it one of the greatest action sequences in cinema. Lupin III is Japanese comfort-anime canon — a bit like James Bond crossed with the Pink Panther. If you have never seen one of the films, The Castle of Cagliostro is the universally recommended starting point in the whole franchise.

osamu-tezuka.context_blurb: Osamu Tezuka is the Japanese cartoonist widely called the 'God of Manga' — the founding figure who transformed Japanese comics from a kids' novelty into a serious storytelling medium. Born in 1928, Tezuka started drawing comics as a boy during World War II, went on to earn a medical degree while already becoming a working cartoonist, and in 1952 he began drawing a series about a bright-eyed robot boy built to look human after a brilliant scientist loses his real son — complete with rocket boots, machine guns in the hips, and lasers in the eyes. That character, Astro Boy, launched Tezuka's career and in 1963 became the first serialized Japanese TV anime, kicking off the whole industry that followed. Tezuka also drew the gender-bending Princess Knight, the medical thriller Black Jack, the lifelong-unfinished philosophical epic that he worked on for decades about an immortal firebird symbol of life, and the historical epic Buddha, among dozens of other series. He died in 1989, but his style — the big-eyed character design, the cinematic page layouts — set the visual grammar every later manga artist still works inside. Hayao Miyazaki famously admires Tezuka's manga while being critical of his anime, calling much of it rushed and cheap.

sailor-moon.context_blurb: Sailor Moon is a Japanese manga created by Naoko Takeuchi, serialized from 1991 to 1997, and the hit anime adaptation that aired on Japanese TV from 1992 to 1997. It stars a clumsy, cry-baby fourteen-year-old Tokyo schoolgirl who turns out to be the reincarnated princess of a lost ancient Moon Kingdom. She transforms into a magical warrior in a short sailor-suit costume with a tiara and heart-tipped weapons, and her teammates — teen girls named after the other planets in the solar system — each transform the same way to fight increasingly cosmic villains across five story arcs. Sailor Moon is widely considered the founding work of the modern 'magical girl' genre and the first global anime hit aimed squarely at girls, dubbed into dozens of languages and broadcast around the world. The American dub famously censored or rewrote entire relationships to fit 1990s network standards (making one lesbian couple into cousins, for instance), and the merchandise alone made Takeuchi one of the richest manga authors in Japanese history. The series has been remade twice as the more manga-faithful Sailor Moon Crystal (2014) and continues to anchor the international magical-girl fandom. If you are starting out, the original 1990s anime is widely available with subtitles today, and it holds up as one of the warmest coming-of-age magical-girl stories ever told.

my-hero-academia.context_blurb: My Hero Academia is a Japanese superhero manga written and drawn by Kohei Horikoshi, beginning in Weekly Shonen Jump in 2014. It is set in a world where almost every child is born with a superpower called a Quirk, and the strongest Quirk-users work as licensed professional heroes who fight villains for a living. The story follows a freckled, green-haired middle-schooler who was born without a Quirk at all, and his dream of attending the nation's top hero-training high school anyway. He catches the attention of the world's number-one hero — a towering, blond, super-muscular man whose famous grin is supposed to make everyone feel safe — and gets taken in as his secret successor. The anime adaptation from Bones studio has run from 2016 onward and has become one of the biggest shonen franchises of its generation. The series is loaded with named classmates, each with a distinctive Quirk, and a long rogue's gallery of villains built around a cracked-skin young leader with grudges against hero society. Be warned: the questions here give away major plot points.

hajime-no-ippo.context_blurb: Hajime no Ippo (literally 'The First Step') is a long-running Japanese boxing manga by George Morikawa — real name Jouji Morikawa — that began serialization in Weekly Shonen Magazine in 1989 and has continued for more than three decades. Three successive anime adaptations have run since 2000. The main character is a shy, mop-haired Japanese high-school boy who helps his widowed mother run her small coastal fishing-charter business. After getting beaten up by bullies and rescued by a passing professional boxer, the boy stumbles into a boxing gym in Tokyo and discovers he actually loves the sport. He is coached by a gruff retired champion and sparred by the gym's star fighters, slowly climbing from a shy amateur through the Japanese pro ranks and eventually toward world-title contenders. The series is considered one of the most technically detailed sports manga ever drawn — Morikawa studied real boxing gyms, cornerwork, training routines, and famous historical bouts to depict every punch — and its best bouts have become touchstones for anime boxing fans worldwide. Be warned: the questions here give away even the specific big-fight twists. If you are interested in boxing or in sports anime generally, the 2000-2002 Hajime no Ippo anime remains the single best gateway into the whole subgenre.

demon-slayer.context_blurb:
Koyoharu Gotouge drew Demon Slayer in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2016 to 2020, and Ufotable in Tokyo turned it into one of the most watched anime ever made. The setting is Japan's Taisho era, around the 1910s: demons eat people after dark, and a secret order of swordsmen hunts them with black blades. A gentle charcoal-seller comes home to find his family killed and his little sister Nezuko the only one alive, half turned into a demon, so he joins the Demon Slayer Corps looking for a cure and carries her on his back in a wooden box. He is Tanjiro Kamado.

He picks up two companions. One is a jumpy blond who weeps and begs to go home and then, the instant terror knocks him out, moves in his sleep as a Thunder Breathing master of appalling speed, and he is Zenitsu Agatsuma. The other was raised in the mountains, wears a boar's head over his face and fights with two chipped blades, and he is Inosuke Hashibira.

Nine elite swordsmen called Hashira stand above the Corps, each with a Breathing Style. The one who spares Tanjiro and Nezuko in the very first chapter wears half a patterned haori, says almost nothing, and is the Water Hashira, Giyu Tomioka. The tall blind man with the prayer beads and the chained flail, reckoned the strongest of the serving pillars, is the Stone Hashira, Gyomei Himejima. Every one of these styles descends from an original invented by a Sengoku-era swordsman called Yoriichi Tsugikuni, which Tanjiro's family had preserved without knowing it as a religious dance: Sun Breathing (Hinokami Kagura).

The villain is the first demon ever made, past a thousand years old, undone by a single ray of sun, hiding in Tokyo as somebody's husband and father and making new demons by mixing his blood into human wounds. He is Muzan Kibutsuji. Twelve lieutenants called the Kizuki serve him in upper and lower ranks.

The 2020 film Mugen Train outgrossed every Japanese film ever made, passing a record Spirited Away had held for twenty years, and the Hashira it puts at the centre, aboard a haunted overnight train, is Kyojuro Rengoku, the Flame Hashira. The demon who kills him had been a martial artist named Hakuji before Muzan turned him, and he is Akaza, Upper Moon Three.

Part of why the fights look the way they do is technique. Ufotable blends drawn cels with carefully tuned computer work, and for Tanjiro's water attacks the studio used a custom CGI-and-2D blend called digital chiaroscuro shading, with hand-painted Japanese-watercolor overlays, first developed for its Fate adaptation in 2011.

The manga closed in May 2020 after a final fight of some eighty chapters. Muzan bites Tanjiro as he dies, turning him for a moment into the strongest demon there has ever been, and the one who gets through to him is his sister Nezuko, who reverses his demon transformation through her own restored humanity. She had won her own humanity back earlier with the help of Lady Tamayo's medicine. Gotouge then gave the cast a quiet epilogue a hundred years on, in modern Tokyo, where the reborn characters live ordinary lives, and the one drawn alone in a cafe with a book is Kanao Tsuyuri's reincarnation, reading a romance novel at a Tokyo cafe.

naruto.context_blurb: Naruto is a Japanese ninja manga written and drawn by Masashi Kishimoto, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1999 to 2014, with a Studio Pierrot anime adaptation that ran from 2002 and continued into the sequel series Naruto Shippuden through 2017. The main character is a loud, orange-jumpsuit-wearing, orphan ninja boy in the Hidden Leaf Village, who everyone treats as a troublemaker because he secretly carries a sealed nine-tailed demonic fox inside himself. He dreams of becoming the village's leader (the Hokage) one day, and climbs toward that goal through missions with his teammates — a brooding rival from an elite clan, a pink-haired classmate — under a lazy silver-haired teacher who hides his left eye under his headband. The series builds out an enormous world of ninja villages, forbidden techniques, legendary teachers (the Three Sannin), and a shadowy criminal organization called the Akatsuki that hunts tailed-beast hosts across the Shinobi World, culminating in a massive final world war. Naruto's mix of ninja action, found-family friendship, and signature spiraling-sphere technique turned it into one of the Big Three Weekly Shonen Jump franchises of its era alongside One Piece and Bleach. If you are starting out, the first few arcs of the anime are generally considered the best — the long filler stretches that come later test even hardcore fans.

one-piece.context_blurb: One Piece is a Japanese pirate manga written and drawn by Eiichiro Oda, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump since July 1997, and the longest-running mega-hit in the magazine's history — now the bestselling manga series ever printed. The story follows a cheerful, straw-hat-wearing young pirate captain whose stretchy rubber body comes from eating a cursed Devil Fruit as a child, and his dream of sailing to the end of the ocean to find a legendary treasure left behind by the executed previous Pirate King. He gathers a crew of specialists — a green-haired three-sword swordsman, a blue-haired navigator, a sharpshooter, a lying cook, a reindeer doctor, an archaeologist, a cyborg shipwright, a skeleton musician — and sails one impossible-ocean island after another, building toward answers about a mysterious hundred-year gap in world history called the Void Century. One Piece has been adapted into a Toei Animation anime since 1999, a 2023 live-action Netflix series, and countless films — but Oda's long serialized manga, which he has promised an eventual ending to, is the heart of the franchise. The series' power system (Haki) and the three-type classification of Devil Fruits are among the most carefully worked out in all of shonen.

bleach.context_blurb:
Tite Kubo drew Bleach in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2001 to 2016, and it made its name on sword designs, long coats and villains with nicknames. An orange-haired high-school boy has always been able to see ghosts. One night a small Soul Reaper called Rukia Kuchiki comes through his bedroom wall chasing a soul-eating monster, is wounded, and passes her powers to him so that he can protect his family, and the boy is Ichigo Kurosaki. The huge cleaver he ends up carrying is a zanpakuto named Zangetsu, and a Soul Reaper's zanpakuto is sealed until its owner speaks its name and its release command.

Behind the living world is the Soul Society, an afterlife built like feudal Japan and guarded by thirteen squads, the Gotei 13, each with a captain. At the start of the story the captain-commander is a scarred old man with a long beard who had founded the whole organisation a thousand years before, Genryusai Shigekuni Yamamoto. His walking cane is not a cane. Toshiro Hitsugaya, the youngest captain the Gotei has ever had, releases an ice dragon with the words reign over the frozen heavens, and the squad he leads is Squad 10.

The arc most readers rate highest is the third and longest, in which Ichigo and his friends break into the Soul Society to reach a condemned comrade before her execution, climbing at last to the tower where she is held: Senzaikyu, the Tower of Penitence atop Sokyoku Hill. It runs about sixty chapters and more than forty episodes, and it ends on one of the best cliffhangers in the series.

The manga ran to 686 chapters, ending in August 2016 with the Thousand-Year Blood War, a war against the Quincy, an ancient people bound up with the Hollows, whose king has waited centuries in a frozen state and is named Yhwach, the soul-stealing Quincy progenitor. Studio Pierrot animated that last arc in three runs between 2022 and 2024, nearly a decade after the comic finished, which is a rare second chance for an anime and worth watching on that account alone.

attack-on-titan.context_blurb:
Hajime Isayama drew Attack on Titan from September 2009 to April 2021, and the premise is a nightmare a child grasps at once: the last of humanity lives inside three rings of enormous stone wall, because outside them walk naked giants that eat people. The outer wall is Maria and the middle one Rose, and the innermost ring, where the king and the capital sit in safety, is named Sina. When something colossal kicks the outer wall open the giants come through, and three young friends enlist, ending up in the Survey Corps, the unit that goes outside.

Their gear is why the action looks like nothing else: an Omni-Directional Mobility rig that fires grapples into a tree or a titan's shoulder and swings the soldier through the air. The badge on their green jackets, one white wing crossed over one blue, got the nickname Wings of Freedom, and Isayama has said he took it from a real unit, the British Royal Air Force's Pathfinder squadron of WWII, whose job of finding targets in the dark matches what the Corps does. The ranks, the boots and the European names come out of the same research.

The anime arrived in 2013, and the first three seasons, the ones people remember for the sky-diving combat, were animated by Wit Studio. MAPPA took the final season from 2020, after Wit turned down the heavy computer work the later titans needed.

The story keeps opening outward. By the fourth season it has crossed the sea to the mainland, where the people behind the walls turn out to be a hated minority, called Eldians, descendants of the Founding Titan's bloodline, kept in internment districts and made to wear armbands. The bloodline runs back two thousand years to one figure remembered as the mother of them all, Ymir Fritz, the slave-girl who made a pact with the Devil of All Earth. Isayama is drawing on 1930s Europe and has never pretended otherwise.

The manga ended in 2021 at 139 chapters, and the Japanese title of the last chapter sends the reader back to a quiet spot from the opening pages; Kodansha's official English rendering is Toward the Tree on That Hill. Readers argued about the finale and are arguing still, which is its own reason to read the thing and decide.

death-note.context_blurb:
Tsugumi Ohba wrote Death Note and Takeshi Obata drew it, in Weekly Shonen Jump between 2003 and 2006, and Madhouse animated it from 2006. A black leather notebook falls out of the sky in Tokyo because a bored death god called Ryuk wants to see what a human will do with it. Anyone whose name is written inside dies, provided the writer can picture the face, and the brilliant, bored schoolboy who picks it up and starts killing criminals with it is Light Yagami. He takes a nickname that is the English word killer run through Japanese sounds, and the press and the police end up calling him Kira.

The police cannot explain a world of dying criminals, so they call in a detective who works through an intermediary, sits crouched on his heels, lives on cake and sweets and will not give a name, going by a single letter: L. He is three top detectives rolled into one identity, and the name itself is a weapon against him, since anyone holding a Death Note could kill him by writing it, which is why almost nobody knows that he is L Lawliet. He was raised at Watari's orphanage, Wammy's House.

The first meeting face to face is a trap on both sides. Light and L are named joint top scorer at an entrance ceremony and introduce themselves under false names, L borrowing the name of a real Japanese pop singer as a private joke, and the place is To-Oh University, fictional Tokyo Imperial-style elite institution. Earlier, in a sequence famous for running both men's inner monologue at once over close-ups of a ball and a racket, each watches the other for a tell: the activity is a televised tennis match Light watches while L watches him watching. In chapter 58 Light works out that he is under close surveillance, lists six lettered contingencies in his head from A to F, and the one he runs is Plan B, the contingency that involved a specific date-marked notebook-page. What he thinks to himself afterwards became one of the most quoted lines in anime.

L does not last the whole story. Two orphans from Wammy's House divide his role between them, one white-haired and fond of marshmallows, the other blond and fond of chocolate, and their names are Near and Mello. Near, whose real name is Nate River, works on the floor among his toys and dice, and the tic Obata drew over and over is that he twists a single lock of his white hair around his index finger.

The book itself was copied from a real object. Obata redrew the cover several times and worked from a prop the publisher's team made for him, a Moleskine-style notebook with custom hand-cut leather cover provided by Shueisha's production team, grain and stitching and page edges and all. If you like a thriller in which almost nothing happens except two people thinking at each other, this is the one everybody recommends first.

fullmetal-alchemist.context_blurb:
Hiromu Arakawa drew Fullmetal Alchemist from 2001 to 2010, and there are two anime: the 2003 one, which overtook the comic and invented an ending, and the 2009 Brotherhood from Studio Bones, which follows her to the last page. The world runs on alchemy, a science of rearranging matter through drawn circles, bound by a law of equivalent exchange in which nothing comes from nothing.

Two brothers break the deepest taboo of that law in an attempt to raise their dead mother. The rebound takes an arm and a leg from the elder and the whole body of the younger, whose soul his brother pins to a hollow suit of armour with a blood seal, and who stops to rescue stray cats wherever he goes; he is Alphonse Elric. The state certifies the elder at twelve, the youngest State Alchemist there has ever been, with a silver pocket watch and the title that names the series: The Fullmetal Alchemist. What the two of them met in the instant the ritual failed was the Gate of Truth, with the entity called Truth at its threshold, which collects the toll in person. It is also why Edward can transmute by clapping his hands instead of drawing a circle: he had seen the Gate of Truth and 'paid the toll' for human transmutation knowledge.

The country the brothers live in is drawn as early-1900s Germany with alchemy where the gunpowder should be, and it is called Amestris. Its state alchemists are soldiers, officially human weapons. The man in the blue uniform who snaps his ignition-cloth gloves to burn an enemy to ash, and who means to climb to the top and pull the regime down from the inside, is Colonel Roy Mustang. He fought in the Ishvalan campaign and has never got over it.

Against them stand seven artificial people named for the deadly sins, made by an ancient homunculus called Father, who intends to swallow every soul in the country at once. The first of them the brothers run into is a tall woman, dark-haired, with a red mark on her chest, and the sin she carries is Lust. Father's design required the nation's wars to be arranged in advance and the army steered from the top, and the Fuhrer who did the steering, himself a homunculus with an eye that reads any opponent's next move, is King Bradley.

Brotherhood ran through five opening themes, and the first of them, the fast rock song called Again, belongs to Yui (a solo artist, not a band), whose 'Again' opens Brotherhood's first arc. Arakawa grew up on a Hokkaido farm and put more theology, and more about war guilt, into a boys' adventure comic than anyone expected it to carry.

hunter-x-hunter.context_blurb: Hunter x Hunter is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yoshihiro Togashi, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump since 1998 — though the author's chronic back pain has forced multiple extended hiatuses stretching years at a time. The main character is a cheerful green-haired twelve-year-old boy raised by his aunt on a tiny island, who learns that the father he never knew is actually a legendary member of a secretive licensed profession called Hunters, and sets off to take the brutal multi-stage Hunter Exam himself. Among the applicants he meets a lanky blond kid studying to become a doctor, a stiff angry teen seeking revenge for his murdered clan, and a soft-spoken white-haired boy who turns out to be the twelve-year-old heir of the world's most famous assassin family. The series has moved through long distinct arcs — the Hunter Exam, Heavens Arena, Yorknew City, Greed Island, the Chimera Ant invasion, and the current Dark Continent plot — and treats its battle system of personalized aura abilities called Nen as one of the most carefully worked-out power systems in all of shonen. Hunter x Hunter is a long game for patient readers — a deep cut that devoted manga fans prize.

jojos-bizarre-adventure.context_blurb: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Hirohiko Araki, serialized almost continuously since 1987 across nine numbered Parts in two Shueisha magazines — one of the longest and most ambitious manga runs in the medium. Each Part is set in a different era (Victorian England, 1930s Egypt, 1980s Japan, 1990s small-town Japan, 2001 Italy, modern Florida) and stars a new member of the Joestar bloodline, who is always known by a nickname that reduces his first name to the two syllables 'JoJo.' Across generations, the Joestars battle supernatural threats — originally a vampire ancestor turned villain, then stand-wielding assassins, then a serial killer in a quiet town, then the Italian mafia. From Part 3 onward, the manga introduced its signature mechanic: fighters wield 'Stands,' invisible-except-to-other-Stand-users spirit companions with individual names (nearly all borrowed from classic rock songs and albums) and bizarre specific powers. Araki's art style — huge muscles, dramatic 1980s fashion-magazine poses — is as iconic as the plots themselves, and the series' catchphrases, menacing-stance panels, and specific Stand ability reveals are endlessly meme-able online. For a new reader, the chronological starting point is 1987's Phantom Blood, but most fans recommend jumping straight into Part 3's 1988 Egypt road trip as the real gateway. The 2012-onward anime adaptation covers the whole saga in rolling batches.

yu-yu-hakusho.context_blurb: Yu Yu Hakusho (literally 'Ghost Files') is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yoshihiro Togashi, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1990 to 1994 and adapted into a 1992-1995 anime by Studio Pierrot. The main character is a tough middle-school delinquent with a black slicked-back pompadour who skips class, brawls, and gambles — until one afternoon he dies while pushing a child out of the path of a speeding car. His selfless death surprises the afterlife, and he is given a chance to come back to life if he will work as a Spirit Detective, policing supernatural threats to the human world. He teams up with a short, white-forelocked demon swordsman, a tall red-haired fox-demon, and his old brawling rival, and the series climaxes in a long arena-tournament arc called the Dark Tournament. Togashi developed the back problems that have slowed Hunter x Hunter for decades during this run, and the series' late arcs ended abruptly as a result. Yu Yu Hakusho was one of the earliest big anime hits to reach American kids on Cartoon Network's Toonami block, where its stylish fights and 90s-shonen aesthetic made it a gateway anime for an entire generation. If you are starting out, the big tournament arc is widely considered the series' peak and is where many fans point newcomers first.

initial-d.context_blurb: Initial D is a Japanese street-racing manga written and drawn by Shuichi Shigeno, serialized in Young Magazine from 1995 to 2013, with a popular 1998 anime adaptation. It is set in the mountains of Gunma Prefecture, Japan, in the 1990s, in a world of late-night downhill touge races on twisty two-lane roads, where small teams of young drivers push their modified cars sideways through hairpin corners at terrifying speed. The main character is a quiet high-school boy who makes nightly tofu-delivery runs down the mountain in his father's beat-up ten-year-old Toyota — unaware that his father, a legendary former touge driver, has been secretly training him into the fastest downhill driver in the prefecture. The series is built around genuine real-world roads, real production-car models, and specific real tuning parts, and the anime made Japan's mountain-pass drifting culture a global phenomenon. Its soundtrack of imported Italian Eurobeat became as recognizable as the series itself. Initial D is foundational canon for the whole modern car-and-anime fandom, and specific driver skills — hand brakes, feint motions, gutter runs — are part of the shared vocabulary. If you like cars, Initial D is the best anime gateway there is — the opening episodes include nighttime drift sequences that have launched a whole generation of real-world car hobbyists.

toilet-bound-hanako-kun.context_blurb: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun (in Japanese, Jibaku Shonen Hanako-kun) is a Japanese supernatural comedy manga written and drawn by the duo Aida Iro, serialized since 2014, with a popular 2020 anime adaptation from studio Lerche. It is set at Kamome Academy, a Japanese high school famous for its Seven Mysteries — ghost stories whispered by students that have turned out to be real resident spirits with their own rules and territories. The protagonist is a shy, superstitious first-year girl who summons a charming boy ghost rumored to haunt the third stall of the old girls' bathroom on the third floor. She asks him for a love potion, accidentally becomes bound to his service, and gets pulled into one strange hauntings-and-mysteries case after another, meeting the other six supernaturals and uncovering the boy ghost's melancholy history, including a mysterious twin brother. The anime is immediately recognizable for its soft pastel watercolor-and-chalk visual style and dreamy Lerche art direction. Be warned: the questions here give away even the deeper reveals about the ghost's past and his twin. If you are starting out, the 2020 anime is widely available with subtitles today and runs through roughly the manga's first six volumes in twelve episodes.

anime-misc-classics.context_blurb:
This one is a shelf rather than a single series: eleven Japanese classics worth hunting down, each with a fandom of its own.

Kazuki Takahashi's 1996 manga puts a shy boy called Yugi Mutou in a place called Domino City, where the game shop belongs to his grandfather Sugoroku, and an ancient Egyptian puzzle turns him into a champion of a card game full of dragons and wizards; the series is Yu-Gi-Oh! Konami launched the real trading-card game off the back of it in 1999, which is why those cards exist at all.

Rumiko Takahashi is among the best-selling comics authors who ever lived, and two of hers are on the shelf. Her first big hit, which ran from 1978 to 1987, starred Lum, a horned alien princess in a tiger-stripe bikini who flew through the air and electrocuted her human fiance Ataru whenever he misbehaved, and its punning title is Urusei Yatsura. The later one drops a schoolgirl named Kagome down a dry shrine well five hundred years into the past, where she meets a silver-haired boy with dog ears who carries an enormous sword and hunts the shards of a broken jewel with her, and that series is Inuyasha.

Yoichi Takahashi began Captain Tsubasa in 1981, about a boy named Tsubasa Ozora who means to play for Japan in a world cup, and the sport is soccer. Lionel Messi, Zinedine Zidane, Andres Iniesta and Fernando Torres have all said the comic shaped them as children, which may be the largest real-world footprint any manga has.

Buronson wrote and Tetsuo Hara drew Fist of the North Star in 1983, set in a nuclear wasteland, where a seven-scarred master of a Chinese-style killing art strikes hidden pressure points and walks away before his enemies burst, and the warrior is Kenshiro. His line about an opponent already being dead is among the most quoted in anime.

Sunrise's Code Geass arrived in 2006. An exiled Britannian prince hiding as a Tokyo schoolboy takes a mind-control power from an immortal green-haired girl called C.C. and raises a masked rebellion against his own family, and the prince is Lelouch. The mask carries a name of its own, and leading the Black Knights against the occupation, his alter ego is Zero.

Gainax made six episodes of FLCL in 2000, the ones people pronounce Fooly Cooly, which open with a pink-haired alien roaring into a sleepy town on a yellow Vespa and clouting a bored twelve-year-old called Naota with a blue electric bass, and she is Haruko. The Pillows did the soundtrack and it outlived the show.

Shinichiro Watanabe followed Cowboy Bebop with Samurai Champloo in 2004, scored in hip-hop by Nujabes, in which a waitress named Fuu gets two rival swordsmen, feral Mugen and stoic Jin, to walk Edo-period Japan with her while she looks for a samurai from her childhood, identified by one odd detail, which is that he smells of sunflowers.

Yuki Urushibara's Mushishi, animated in 2005, is the quiet one. A white-haired traveller called Ginko walks old rural Japan with a wooden medicine chest, treating people harmed by half-visible primal creatures that are neither plant nor animal and that most people cannot see, and the show calls them mushi. They gather around Ginko wherever he goes, which puts everyone near him at risk, and his defence is a habit: he smokes constantly to suppress the mushi he naturally attracts.

Takehiko Inoue drew Slam Dunk between 1990 and 1996, in which a red-haired troublemaker in his first year, Hanamichi Sakuragi, joins the basketball team in Kanagawa to impress a classmate, and his school is Shohoku. Inoue storyboarded and directed the 2022 animated film himself. Akira Toriyama's gag comic Dr. Slump and Bandai's Digimon round out the shelf.

princess-bride.context_blurb: The Princess Bride is a 1987 American fantasy comedy film directed by Rob Reiner and written by William Goldman — adapted from Goldman's own 1973 fantasy novel of the same name, which is itself famously framed as the 'abridgement' of a much longer work by a fictional author named S. Morgenstern. The movie is told as a bedtime story, with a grandfather (Peter Falk) reading to his sick grandson (a young Fred Savage), about a poor farm boy named Westley who falls in love with a beautiful farm girl named Buttercup, loses her to pirates, and comes back years later disguised as a mysterious masked swordsman to rescue her from an evil prince's wedding. The cast is a who's-who of 1980s talent: Cary Elwes as Westley, Robin Wright as Buttercup, Mandy Patinkin as the Spanish swordsman Inigo Montoya seeking vengeance for his father, the French giant Andre the Giant as the friendly brute Fezzik, Wallace Shawn as a bald loudmouth Sicilian mastermind, Billy Crystal and Carol Kane as a bickering old miracle-maker couple. It is one of the most quotable comedies ever made and its plot has passed into common knowledge. Many kids have had the whole script memorized since fourth grade.

back-to-the-future.context_blurb:
Back to the Future came out in 1985, directed by Robert Zemeckis, written with Bob Gale and produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin. A California teenager gets thrown back to 1955, interrupts the night his parents met, and has to repair his own family history before he fades out of a Polaroid. The machine that takes him there is a stainless-steel car with gull-wing doors, a DeLorean DMC-12, picked because Zemeckis wanted something that would look like a spaceship to 1955 eyes. It needs 88 miles an hour and a flux capacitor.

Doc Brown, played by Christopher Lloyd, greets every impossibility in all three films by grabbing his white hair and shouting two old-fashioned words: Great Scott! He says it in 1955, in 1985, in the 2015 of the second film and in the 1885 of the third.

The casting nearly went another way. Zemeckis shot four or five weeks with a serious young actor in the lead, then decided he was too dramatic for a comedy, and that actor was Eric Stoltz. Amblin paid him in full and reshot almost everything. The actor who took over the part was Michael J. Fox. He was tied to the sitcom Family Ties, so he filmed at night and at weekends for months, sleeping in his car between sets.

The jokes are built to pay off. Marty lands in 1955 in a red puffer vest of a kind nobody there has ever seen, and the locals decide it is a life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat). Reading his underwear label, they start calling him Calvin Klein. In the diner he asks for a Tab, which was Coca-Cola's diet brand, and then for a Pepsi Free, and the gag is that Tab and Pepsi Free, both soft drinks of 1985, mean nothing at all to a soda clerk in 1955, who tells him he cannot have a tab unless he orders something.

The locations and the stunts were real. The mall where the DeLorean makes its first jump is Puente Hills Mall in Industry, California (despite often being misidentified as Burbank), and the Twin Pines turning into Lone Pine on Marty's return is one of the film's small payoffs. The clock tower stands on the Universal backlot, on a courthouse set built in 1962 for To Kill a Mockingbird, and the cable-swinging climax looks lethal because of a trick: the cable was attached to Lloyd's stunt double via a hidden harness, and a pulley counterweight system did most of the swing motion.

The second film, in 1989, guessed at 21 October 2015 and filled it with hoverboards, self-lacing Nikes and a nineteenth Jaws sequel on a cinema hoarding. One guess landed, and it startled Bob Gale when it did: the Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction), ending the longest drought in American sport. Start with the 1985 film; the other two only make sense after it.

ghostbusters.context_blurb:
Ghostbusters came out in 1984, directed by Ivan Reitman and written by two of its stars, Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis. Three parapsychologists lose their university posts and open a commercial ghost-removal business in a disused Manhattan firehouse, with proton packs and traps of their own making, and a fourth man joins them for wages. The job ends on a rooftop against a Sumerian god who demands that they name the form of their own destructor, at which point Ray thinks of the most harmless thing he knows and a hundred-foot mascot in a sailor hat comes up Fifth Avenue: The Stay-Puft Marshmallow Man.

Aykroyd wrote the script with three friends in mind for the parts, one of them John Belushi, who died in March 1982 before a frame was shot. Bill Murray took the part of Peter Venkman and played it, Aykroyd has said, as a tribute to the energy Belushi had brought to Animal House (1978) and The Blues Brothers (1980) — Belushi's Bluto/Jake energy translated into Venkman. Eddie Murphy, also in the original plan, had Beverly Hills Cop to make, and the part written for him became Winston Zeddemore, played by Ernie Hudson.

The marshmallow man was a man in a suit. The stuntman Bill Bryan wore it on a tabletop New York, shot to make him look a hundred feet tall, and the effects were run by the man behind Poltergeist and Return of the Jedi, Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios. That sequence cost more than every other effect in the film put together.

Ray Parker Jr's theme spent three weeks at the top of the Billboard chart and then went to court, because Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court. The settlement carried a confidentiality clause that Lewis later broke in an interview, and he was sued over that in turn.

The 1989 sequel sends a river of pink slime under Manhattan, fed by bad temper, and its villain is a sixteenth-century Carpathian tyrant living inside his own portrait, played by a German former professional boxer who acted under the name Wilhelm von Homburg (real name Norbert Grupe). Reitman had Max von Sydow dub the lines. The climax turns the Statue of Liberty into a weapon, and the trick is that the team plays 'Higher and Higher' by Jackie Wilson to charge the slime with positive emotions.

The Saturday-morning cartoon began in 1986 under J. Michael Straczynski, who later made Babylon 5 and who did not want the green ghost Slimer promoted to a regular. ABC insisted, the ratings agreed, and from 1988 the show was called Slimer! and the Real Ghostbusters. Straczynski quit that year.

scott-pilgrim.context_blurb: Scott Pilgrim is a six-volume black-and-white Canadian graphic novel series written and drawn by Bryan Lee O'Malley, published from 2004 to 2010, and adapted into the 2010 live-action film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, directed by British filmmaker Edgar Wright and starring Michael Cera. The series is set in Toronto, Canada, and follows a broke 23-year-old bass player in a struggling indie rock band who falls for a mysterious American delivery girl with constantly-changing hair color — only to discover that in order to date her he has to defeat her seven evil exes in literal video-game-style combat, complete with floating pixel-art hit points, coins, extra lives, and power-ups. The books and film treat the whole twenty-something Toronto music-scene milieu as a video game come to life, loaded with references to Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, Street Fighter II, Final Fantasy, and dozens of other classics. The 2010 film was a financial disappointment on release but has since become a huge cult favorite, and a 2023 anime series adapted the full comic story on Netflix with the original movie cast returning as voice actors. Be warned: the questions here give away the plot. If you grew up on classic video games, Scott Pilgrim is almost designed as a gift — every page and scene is a reference to a classic game or band.

super-mario-bros-movie-2023.context_blurb: The Super Mario Bros. Movie is a 2023 animated feature film produced by Illumination and Nintendo, based on Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. video-game series. It made over one billion dollars at the global box office. The film opens in Brooklyn, New York, where the Italian-American plumber brothers Mario (voiced by Chris Pratt) and Luigi (Charlie Day) have just launched their own plumbing business and get sucked through a city sewer pipe into the fantastical Mushroom Kingdom. Mario meets its ruler, Princess Peach, who is defending her kingdom from the invading koopa king Bowser (voiced by Jack Black) and his massive army. Mario trains to fight back, picks up his signature power-ups, teams up with Donkey Kong and the Kong tribe, and races to rescue his captured brother. The film is loaded with deep-cut references for players of the Nintendo games — specific levels, specific power-ups, specific musical cues from the 1985 original and later entries — and plays as a love letter to classic Nintendo. Be warned: the questions here give away the plot of the 2023 film. Jack Black's piano ballad from the film became an unexpected real-world top-forty radio hit.

terminator-franchise.context_blurb: The Terminator is an American science-fiction action film franchise created by Canadian director James Cameron, who conceived the first script in the early 1980s and famously sold it to a producer for one dollar on the condition that he would get to direct it himself. The 1984 original stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as a killer cyborg sent back from a dystopian post-nuclear-war future, hunting a Los Angeles waitress whose unborn son will one day lead humanity's resistance against the machines. The 1991 sequel Terminator 2: Judgment Day flips the formula — Schwarzenegger's model is now a reprogrammed protector guarding the waitress's teenage son against a far more advanced shape-shifting liquid-metal cyborg. T2 was one of the first blockbusters to lean heavily on computer-generated imagery (CGI), with Industrial Light & Magic developing custom morphing software for the liquid-metal effects. The franchise has produced several later sequels and TV spinoffs that fans debate, but the first two Cameron films are the canonical pair — and Schwarzenegger's two-word tagline from the 1984 original has become one of the most-quoted lines in cinema. His casting is itself legend — Cameron originally considered giving him a different lead role in the film. If you are starting out, the 1984 original and 1991 sequel are the two to see — in that order — before any of the later entries.

karate-kid.context_blurb: The Karate Kid is a 1984 American martial-arts drama film directed by John G. Avildsen (who had already won a Best Director Oscar for the 1976 boxing film Rocky) and starring Ralph Macchio as the teenage protagonist Daniel LaRusso. The story opens with Daniel moving with his widowed mother from New Jersey to Reseda in southern California, where he quickly becomes the bullying target of a gang of boys from a cruel local karate dojo called Cobra Kai. He is secretly taken under the wing of his apartment building's gentle Japanese-American handyman Mr. Miyagi (played by Pat Morita, whose own real backstory echoes Miyagi's wartime scenes), who trains him in Okinawan karate through chore-based muscle-memory drills — waxing cars, painting fences, sanding decks — and prepares him to defeat the bullies at the All-Valley Karate Tournament. The film built the whole 'wise mentor and unlikely-student' sports-drama template, launched a 1980s franchise of sequels, and inspired the long-running sequel streaming series Cobra Kai starting in 2018. Specific moves and lines from the tournament sequence have been quoted and parodied by nearly every sports film made since. If you are interested in martial arts or in classic sports films, The Karate Kid is widely considered the best 1980s starting point there is.

top-gun.context_blurb: Top Gun is a 1986 American aerial-combat drama directed by Tony Scott (the younger brother of Ridley Scott), produced by Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, and starring Tom Cruise. The film opens with a cocky young U.S. Naval fighter aviator named Pete Mitchell being accepted into the elite fighter-weapons school at Naval Air Station Miramar in southern California — the real Navy school known in the Pentagon as 'Top Gun' — alongside his back-seater and his hotshot rival pilots. Mitchell flies the F-14 Tomcat, pulls high-speed maneuvers around aircraft carriers, falls for a civilian flight instructor played by Kelly McGillis, and lives through a mid-air disaster that forces him to decide whether he still wants to fly. The film was shot on a budget that was unusually high for a non-effects-driven movie at the time, with the U.S. Navy loaning actual F-14s and carriers for filming. It became the highest-grossing film of 1986, launched Cruise's career as an action star, and its Kenny Loggins theme song 'Danger Zone' became one of the most iconic needle-drops in cinema. A 2022 legacy sequel starring Cruise, Top Gun: Maverick, followed thirty-six years later. If you are interested in military aviation or in classic 1980s action, Top Gun is foundational viewing — and the 2022 sequel is the rare legacy follow-up most fans agree improves on the original.

the-goonies.context_blurb: The Goonies is a 1985 American kids-adventure film directed by Richard Donner (who had already made The Omen in 1976 and Superman in 1978), produced by Steven Spielberg, and written by Chris Columbus from a story Spielberg sketched out. The film is set in Astoria, Oregon, in the real coastal Pacific Northwest. A gang of middle-school friends living in a neighborhood called the Goon Docks are about to lose their homes to a developer bulldozing them for a country-club golf course. In the family attic, the asthmatic protagonist Mikey (played by a young Sean Astin, who would later play Samwise Gamgee in the Lord of the Rings films) and his friends find a 300-year-old treasure map pointing to a pirate's buried fortune hidden in a cave network beneath their town. They sneak off to find it, pursued by a comic trio of criminal fugitives. The film also features Josh Brolin, Corey Feldman, Jonathan Ke Quan, and a huge beloved monster-ally called Sloth, and its Cyndi Lauper theme song was a hit single. It remains the defining Spielberg-era kids'-treasure-hunt movie, and specific scenes — the Fratelli family hideout, the pirate ship, the 'truffle shuffle' — are part of the shared childhood vocabulary of several generations.

et-the-extra-terrestrial.context_blurb:
Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial opened in 1982, written by Melissa Mathison, with Henry Thomas as Elliott and a seven-year-old Drew Barrymore as his sister. A three-foot alien is left behind by his own ship in a California suburb and hides in a tool shed, and the boy coaxes him indoors with a trail of sweets up the stairs. Mars turned down the chance to use M&Ms, Hershey paid a million dollars instead, and the candy on the lawn is Reese's Pieces. It is the most cited product placement in the history of the movies, because sales tripled, making it one of the most successful product placements in film history.

The video game is the other half of the legend. Atari paid upwards of twenty million dollars for the licence, ordered five million cartridges, and gave the whole job to one in-house programmer with about five weeks to deliver before Christmas, and that programmer was Howard Scott Warshaw. He had designed Yars' Revenge the same year and still defends the game. Only a third of the cartridges sold. Trucks hauled the rest into a desert landfill and buried them under concrete, and the city was Alamogordo. Everybody treated that as an urban legend until a documentary crew dug the site up in April 2014 and found the cartridges exactly where the story said they were.
