indiana-jones.context_blurb: Indiana Jones is an American adventure film franchise created by George Lucas and Steven Spielberg, launched in 1981 with Raiders of the Lost Ark. Harrison Ford stars as Dr. Henry 'Indiana' Jones Jr., a globe-trotting archaeology professor who divides his life between classroom lectures and whip-cracking, bull-whip-wielding, Nazi-fighting treasure hunts for ancient religious artifacts, wearing his iconic brown leather jacket and brown wide-brimmed hat. Raiders (1981) sends him racing the Nazis to the Ark of the Covenant in 1936 Egypt and Nepal; the darker 1984 prequel Temple of Doom pits him against a Thuggee death-cult in India with a spunky Chinese-American kid sidekick named Short Round (played by a young Jonathan Ke Quan); and the 1989 Last Crusade teams Indy with his crusty medievalist father (played by Sean Connery, in a part Spielberg conceived to evoke 'James Bond as the father of Indiana Jones') on a hunt for the Holy Grail in Petra, Jordan. Two later entries followed, but the original 1981-1989 trilogy is the canonical heart of the series — a pulp-magazine-inspired, Saturday-matinee love letter that defined blockbuster adventure for the whole 1980s. If you have never seen the films, the 1981 original is the right starting point — it is still widely regarded as the best action-adventure movie ever made.

schwarzenegger-80s-action.context_blurb: Arnold Schwarzenegger's action films defined 1980s and early-1990s American blockbuster cinema, even with the Terminator films set aside. The three big ones here are John Milius's 1982 fantasy Conan the Barbarian, in which Schwarzenegger plays Robert E. Howard's muscular Cimmerian wandering warrior Conan hunting a snake-cult wizard named Thulsa Doom (played by James Earl Jones) who murdered his parents; John McTiernan's 1987 jungle sci-fi-horror Predator, in which Schwarzenegger leads a special-forces team being picked off one by one by an invisible alien trophy-hunter in a Central American jungle; and Paul Verhoeven's 1990 Mars-based thriller Total Recall, in which Schwarzenegger plays a construction worker whose implanted vacation memories either are or are not fake. All three were shaped by their towering, Austrian-accented leading man and by the practical-effects and jungle-shooting conditions of their era, and all three leaned hard into huge-weapon action, memorable one-liners, and physical sets rather than later-era digital effects. Basil Poledouris's choral-and-anvil score for Conan the Barbarian is one of the most imitated fantasy soundtracks ever recorded. If you are curious about the whole 1980s action-film era, these three films together give a complete tour of what Schwarzenegger meant to the decade.

alien-franchise.context_blurb:
Alien began in 1979 with Ridley Scott's film about the crew of a deep-space towing ship, the Nostromo, who answer a distress call and bring something aboard. It was sold on one of the great taglines, which promised that in space nobody would hear you scream. The creature came from a Swiss surrealist painter whom Scott hired after seeing his airbrushed art book Necronomicon, and the painter was Hans Ruedi Giger, who signed his work with his initials. Giger's biomechanical style, skeleton fused with machine, set the look of everything that followed, and it won him an Oscar.

James Cameron's sequel in 1986 changed the genre without changing the universe, turning a haunted-house picture into a war picture. The warrant officer from the first film wakes after decades of frozen sleep and goes back to LV-426 with a squad of Colonial Marines, and the character Sigourney Weaver played across four of these films is Ellen Ripley. The colony they reach is empty except for one child who has been living in the air ducts, and her family had named her Rebecca, but her brother called her Newt (real name Rebecca Jorden) because she could fit into all the small places. Carrie Henn, who played her, never made another film.

The hardware was real, which is why it still looks right. Stan Winston's team built the Alien Queen as a costume that stood fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement, with a rod-and-puppet crew of a dozen more off camera. Weaver, after a few rehearsals, insisted on driving the yellow power loader herself. Jonesy the cat was played by four trained cats.

Shooting at Pinewood went badly at first. Cameron wanted the pace he was used to in America, the British crew was used to another, and the story that gets retold is that he sacked the lot of them on day one. What happened is less cinematic: Cameron actually held his ground until the crew, expecting to be fired, came back, and the film was made. It cost about eighteen million dollars, drew seven Oscar nominations, won two, and earned Weaver a Best Actress nomination, which nobody expects for a film with xenomorphs in it.

Everyone assumed he would go straight on to a third. He did not, because Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel, and the 1992 third film went instead to a young David Fincher. The 1979 original and the 1986 sequel are the pair to watch, in that order, on the same night if you can take it.

star-wars-original-trilogy.context_blurb: The original Star Wars trilogy is three American science-fantasy films — A New Hope (1977), The Empire Strikes Back (1980), and Return of the Jedi (1983) — written by George Lucas, produced by his company Lucasfilm, and distributed by 20th Century Fox. The story is set in a galaxy far, far away, in an ongoing war between the authoritarian Galactic Empire and the Rebel Alliance that is trying to overthrow it. In A New Hope, a farmboy named Luke Skywalker living on a desert planet with two suns receives a hidden message from a princess being held captive aboard the Empire's planet-destroying battle station, is trained briefly by an old hermit knight in the mystical energy field called the Force, and joins up with a smuggler, a Wookiee, and two droids to attack the station. The Empire Strikes Back introduces the swamp-dwelling little green Jedi Master Yoda and ends on the most famous family-reveal twist in cinema history. The main plot beats of these three films have crossed into universal common knowledge. The 1977 original was scored by John Williams and performed by the London Symphony Orchestra, a choice that reshaped Hollywood film music for decades.

tombstone-wyatt-earp.context_blurb: Tombstone is a 1993 American Western film directed by George P. Cosmatos (though the film's chaotic production has been widely credited to star Kurt Russell doing much of the actual directing) and starring Russell as Marshal Wyatt Earp and Val Kilmer in a career-defining supporting turn as the gambler, dentist, and lethal gunfighter 'Doc' Holliday — John Henry Holliday, who was dying of tuberculosis in real life throughout the events depicted. The film dramatizes real historical events in 1881 Arizona Territory: the Earp brothers (Wyatt, Virgil, Morgan) and Doc Holliday arrive in the silver-mining boomtown of Tombstone, clash with a loose gang of cattle rustlers known as the Cowboys, fight the thirty-second October 26 shootout at the O.K. Corral vacant lot that made them legends, and ride out the Vendetta Ride after one of the brothers is killed. The screenplay was written by Kevin Jarre, who also wrote the Civil War film Glory. The real Wyatt Earp lived decades longer, befriended early Hollywood cowboy stars Tom Mix and a young John Wayne, and died in Los Angeles in 1929. The real Doc Holliday died of tuberculosis in Glenwood Springs, Colorado in November 1887. If you are interested in American history or in classic Westerns, Tombstone is one of the great gateway films — Val Kilmer's performance alone is reason to see it.

blade-runner.context_blurb:
Blade Runner opened in June 1982, directed by Ridley Scott and taken loosely from a 1968 novel by Philip K. Dick. Rick Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, is a worn-out ex-policeman in a Los Angeles of rain and neon whose job is to hunt manufactured people the Tyrell Corporation builds for labour in the off-world colonies, and the film's name for them is Replicants. Four of them have come back to Earth illegally.

Dick's novel carries one of the great titles, asking whether androids dream of electric sheep, and it is set in a world where the real animals have nearly gone and people keep electric pets to feel less alone. Almost none of that survives into the film, which borrowed its own name from an unrelated book, and the film the novel became is Blade Runner. Hampton Fancher wrote the first screenplay and David Peoples rewrote it. Dick saw twenty minutes of a rough cut late in 1981, was moved by it, and died of a stroke in March 1982, three months before the opening.

The sound of the film is one enormous keyboard. Vangelis, who had an Oscar in hand for Chariots of Fire, built nearly every cue on a rare Japanese synthesizer weighing something like two hundred pounds, and the instrument is The Yamaha CS-80.

The most quoted speech in science-fiction cinema came from neither screenwriter. Rutger Hauer, playing the replicant Roy Batty, cut the scripted lines right down and added the image of moments vanishing like tears in rain, and he did that writing the night before shooting, in his hotel room. The crew is said to have applauded the take. The fullest account of how it happened is in Future Noir, the definitive making-of book, whose author is Paul Sammon.

The release itself was a mess. Test audiences in Denver and in Dallas turned hostile in May 1982, confused by the pacing and the absence of narration, so Warner Bros. made Scott add a Harrison Ford voiceover, which Ford is reported to have delivered flatly on purpose in the hope that it would be dropped. The studio also tacked on a 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining, aerial shots over forest that Kubrick had never used. The 1992 Director's Cut and the 2007 Final Cut removed both. Find the Final Cut: almost everything cyberpunk looks the way it looks because of this film.

don-bluth.context_blurb:
Don Bluth joined Walt Disney Animation in 1955 as a teenage in-betweener on Sleeping Beauty, rose to lead animator on The Rescuers, and walked out on 13 September 1979 with a dozen or more senior artists behind him. His grievance was craft: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail. Hand inking had gone, and so had the depth of the old multi-plane shots. The film the team abandoned mid-production was The Fox and the Hound (released 1981).

His own studio's first feature came in 1982, a grim fantasy in which a widowed field mouse looks for help for a sick child before the farmer's plough reaches her home, and it is The Secret of NIMH. Those letters stand for a real government laboratory. It follows a 1971 Newbery Medal novel about rats made clever by experiments, Mrs Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, whose author was Robert C. O'Brien. Bluth changed Frisby to Brisby to keep clear of a flying-disc trademark.

In 1983 he drew an arcade game. Cinematronics shipped a cabinet that played hand-drawn cartoon off a laserdisc while the player jabbed the joystick or the sword button on cue to steer a clumsy knight called Dirk the Daring past dragons, collapsing floors and spike traps, and the game is Dragon's Lair. The man who drew it, whose Disney pedigree is why it looked like a feature film, is Don Bluth. The woman Dirk is trying to reach is Princess Daphne. His team worked seven months and drew approximately 50,000 cels — three times the count of a typical 80-minute Disney feature, since a branching game must animate scenes most players never see. It took fifty cents a play against the usual quarter and queues formed anyway, yet arcade owners still lost money, because the laserdiscs wore out after roughly 10,000 plays and machines required constant repair. Sega published the follow-up in 1984, a space opera on the same technology, called Space Ace. Forty years on, it is the cabinet Dustin covets in Stranger Things, where the player logged as MADMAX takes his high score and turns out to be Maxine 'Max' Mayfield.

Steven Spielberg's Amblin then backed two Bluth features. The 1986 one follows a young mouse separated from his family on the crossing to America in the 1880s, and it is An American Tail (1986), about Russian-Jewish mice immigrating to America. The flight is historical, since the family is running from the Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews. Fievel is named for Spielberg's own grandfather, whose surname was Posner. The hit song, a duet across the New York night sky that reached the Billboard top five, got its depth the old way, from a multi-plane camera, the same technology Bluth had championed at Disney before his 1979 defection.

The 1988 one sends a young dinosaur called Littlefoot across a dying landscape after his mother's death, and the child who spoke every one of his lines was no star but Gabriel Damon, a 12-year-old child actor. Test screenings with children went so badly that Universal, with Spielberg and George Lucas, cut approximately 12 minutes, including a more graphic Sharptooth (T-Rex) attack and a longer death sequence for Littlefoot's mother. What was released runs sixty-nine minutes.

In 1989 Bluth made a hand-drawn musical set in the New Orleans of the 1930s about a German Shepherd gangster called Charlie B. Barkin, voiced by Burt Reynolds, and it is All Dogs Go to Heaven. Reynolds took the part for a private reason: his pet Doberman 'Bruno' had recently died, and the part connected him to processing the loss. It opened on 17 November 1989 against Disney's The Little Mermaid and was flattened.

One Disney picture of that decade gets blamed on Bluth and had nothing to do with him. The 1985 adaptation of Lloyd Alexander's Prydain books, with its undead army and its Horned King, was the first Disney cartoon feature to be rated above G, and the film that broke the streak was The Black Cauldron itself, in 1985. Bluth had been gone six years.

westerns-and-old-west-lore.context_blurb: The classic American Western film genre grew out of the real historical Old West figures who inspired it. The best-known 1930s-1960s Western film star was John Wayne, born Marion Robert Morrison in Winterset, Iowa in 1907, who starred in dozens of films by director John Ford including the 1939 breakthrough Stagecoach and the 1956 masterpiece The Searchers, both filmed in Monument Valley on the Arizona-Utah border. In the 1960s the Italian director Sergio Leone reinvented the genre with his three 'Dollars' films starring American actor Clint Eastwood as the Man with No Name — A Fistful of Dollars, For a Few Dollars More, and the three-way-standoff epic The Good, the Bad and the Ugly — followed by the sweeping 1968 Once Upon a Time in the West. The real figures the films draw on include the lawman Wyatt Earp, his tuberculosis-ridden dentist friend Doc Holliday, the gunfighters Wild Bill Hickok (shot dead in Deadwood holding aces-and-eights in 1876) and Jesse James, the outlaw Billy the Kid of New Mexico Territory's Lincoln County War, the outlaw-pair Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, and Buffalo Bill Cody's touring 1883-1913 Wild West Show. Later Westerns include Clint Eastwood's 1985 Pale Rider, his 1992 Oscar-winning Unforgiven, and Kevin Costner's 1990 Dances with Wolves, as well as the 1960 American remake The Magnificent Seven (adapted from a 1954 Akira Kurosawa epic).

saturday-morning-cartoons.context_blurb: The beloved Saturday-morning and after-school American animated TV cartoons of the 1980s and 1990s were a golden age, when every kid grew up on the same shared pool of talking turtles, transforming robots, mythic warriors, cereal commercials, and giant mega-robots. The 1980s wave was driven by toy companies partnering with animation studios like Filmation, Hanna-Barbera, and Rankin/Bass to launch half-hour cartoons tied to action-figure lines: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1987), ThunderCats (1985), the Transformers (1984), G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero (1985), He-Man and the Masters of the Universe (1983), She-Ra: Princess of Power (1985), Voltron (1984), Inspector Gadget (1983), M.A.S.K. (1985), SilverHawks (1986), and BraveStarr (1987). Disney launched its Afternoon syndicated block (DuckTales 1987, Darkwing Duck 1991, TaleSpin 1990, Gargoyles 1994). Warner Bros. revived its characters with Tiny Toon Adventures (1990), Animaniacs (1993), Freakazoid! (1995), and the landmark Batman: The Animated Series (1992). Fox Kids ran the hugely successful X-Men animated series starting in 1992, Spider-Man in 1994, and Nickelodeon launched its own line (Rugrats 1991, The Ren & Stimpy Show 1991, Doug 1991, Hey Arnold! 1996, Recess 1997). Captain Planet (1990) added environmental messaging to the mix, and the Looney Tunes continued to run across decades of reruns.

christmas-and-holiday-specials.context_blurb:
A Charlie Brown Christmas went out on CBS on 9 December 1965, and the network hated it in advance for being slow and sad, with no laugh track, real children's voices, jazz and scripture. Charlie Brown is sent for a tree, walks past the aluminium ones and brings back a scrawny little pine sapling. The jazz piano trio belongs to Vince Guaraldi, who wrote Linus and Lucy and scored the Peanuts films until 1976. Linus recites Luke 2 to explain what Christmas is about, and in the middle of it he drops his blanket at the line 'Fear not'. Schulz had insisted on all of it. The ratings answered them, because it got the second-highest Nielsen rating of the entire week, with 45 percent of all American TVs, and CBS ran it each December until 2019.

The stop-motion ones came from one small outfit. Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer arrived in December 1964, and the studio behind it, and behind Frosty too, is Rankin/Bass. The 1970 Rankin/Bass hour about how Santa first came to town gives grey Sombertown a pompous mayor who outlaws toys, and he is Burgermeister Meisterburger. The 1974 one about a year with no Santa sets the Heat Miser and the Snow Miser singing at each other until their mother settles it, and she is Mother Nature. How the Grinch Stole Christmas! came out as a rhyming picture book in 1957 and as a Chuck Jones half-hour in 1966 narrated by Boris Karloff, and the pen name on it was Dr. Seuss.

A Christmas Story, 1983, puts Ralphie Parker in 1940s Indiana wanting one present while every adult warns that he will shoot his eye out, and what he wants is A Red Ryder BB gun. His father wins a Major Award, a lamp shaped like a leg in a fishnet stocking, and reads what is stamped on the crate aloud as though it were a word: FRAGILE — and the father reads it as 'fra-GEE-lay, must be Italian'. The prop was built for the film in Cleveland, and at a 2014 auction the original fetched Over $100,000 — to a private collector.

National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, 1989, hands a suburban father a disastrous holiday and a bonus envelope holding A one-year membership in the Jelly of the Month Club. The actor playing Clark Griswold, for the third time in the series, is Chevy Chase.

Home Alone, 1990, strands an eight-year-old when his family flies to Paris, and the boy who defends the house with paint cans and glue is Kevin McCallister. John Hughes wrote it, and the director, who later made the first two Harry Potter films, is Chris Columbus. The old neighbour the other children call the South Bend Shovel Slayer is really Old Man Marley, named for the ghost in A Christmas Carol. The house is real: 671 Lincoln Avenue, Winnetka, Illinois, where fans still turn up.

Elf, 2003, sends Will Ferrell out of the North Pole in yellow tights, and its director, who launched Iron Man in 2008, is Jon Favreau.

The Nightmare Before Christmas belongs to both holidays. It began as a three-page poem Tim Burton wrote at Disney in 1982, and it was a Dr. Seuss-style rhyming poem, much shorter and not yet sung. Burton designed and produced the 1993 film but was busy with Batman Returns, so the three years of frame-by-frame animation were run by Henry Selick. Chris Sarandon spoke Jack Skellington; the singing voice, and all ten songs, came from Danny Elfman. Disney thought the thing too dark for its own name and put it out through Touchstone Pictures.

The Polar Express, 2004, is Robert Zemeckis's motion-capture version of Chris Van Allsburg's 1985 book, and Tom Hanks performed six separate roles in it, the conductor and Santa among them. The child has no name in the book and none in the film either, where he is credited as Hero Boy (his actual given name is never used in the film either).

Garfield's Halloween Adventure, 1985, frightened a generation with an old fellow in a shack whispering a warning as midnight strikes: They're coming, they're coming, they're coming. Fans spent decades crediting that voice to Orson Welles, who had nothing to do with it; the credited storyteller is Pat Carroll, later famous as Ursula in The Little Mermaid.

And the argument that never ends: Die Hard, 1988, happens at a Christmas party, and at his 2018 roast Bruce Willis declared that Die Hard is not a Christmas movie.

arcade-golden-age.context_blurb:
The quarter-munching era opens in 1972, when Atari dropped two paddles and a bouncing square into bars and pizza parlours: Pong. The co-founder who ran that project, and who later built the pizza-and-animatronic-mouse chain Chuck E. Cheese, was Nolan Bushnell. Five years on the arcade came home in a wood-grain box from Atari, which called the machine the VCS (Video Computer System) until the 5200 made it the 2600. One cartridge hid the first known Easter egg, a programmer's name walled up in a secret room: Adventure. Another, a shooter about a fly gnawing at a force field, ran a band of boiling static down the middle called The Neutral Zone. Nearly all of it thought with the same cheap eight-bit brain, the MOS Technology 6502.

Japan answered in 1978: Tomohiro Nishikado's marching aliens emptied pockets so fast that the country was said to run short of The 100-yen coin. In 1980 the pizza with one slice gone gave Namco's Toru Iwatani his hero: Pac-Man, who is Yellow and hungry and hunted by Four ghosts; the aggressive one who takes the shortest path is Blinky. Boston students at General Computer hacked the board into a bootleg called Crazy Otto, and once Midway licensed it the hack became Ms. Pac-Man; the engineers were Doug Macrae and Kevin Curran. Namco's swooping-formation line ran from Galaxian in 1979 to Galaga in 1981, which hides the most patient secret in the arcade: spare The blue aliens at bottom — The two blue aliens of the bottom row — fire nothing for a quarter of an hour, and the fleet never shoots again. Namco also buried a pump-wielding digger in colored dirt: Dig Dug.

Nintendo's turn came in 1981. Shigeru Miyamoto wanted a sailor, his sweetheart and a bully from the funny pages, Popeye, lost the licence, and built his own ape instead; the woman on the girders is Pauline, and the carpenter was renamed Mario (after Mario Segale) by the 1982 sequel. The Famicom opened in Japan with three ports: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye.

The Midwest built the hard stuff. Stern's talking maze-shooter with the unkillable bouncing smiley was Berzerk. Williams handed Eugene Jarvis the sideways rescue shooter Defender, whose panel demanded Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick, and then the twin-stick meat grinder Robotron: 2084. John Newcomer made the flap-to-fly duel Joust, player one on an ostrich and player two on a stork, with buzzards under the enemy knights. Atari drew Asteroids in glowing vectors in 1979, and Centipede's trackball came from one of the era's few women designers, Dona Bailey. Konami walked a frog through traffic in Frogger, whose home port shipped with a bonus: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game. Gottlieb's long-nosed orange hopper cursed in punctuation, A cartoon-curse symbol cloud (@!#?@!).

Then the counters ran out. Pac-Man's fruit table overflows at Level 256; Donkey Kong's bonus timer breaks at Level 22. The 1983 crash sent two Atari embarrassments into a New Mexico landfill: the movie tie-in, and Atari 2600 Pac-Man. Score chasing filled the silence. Billy Mitchell ate a perfect 3,333,360 in 1999 at Funspot in Weirs Beach, NH, answered Steve Wiebe's million with a couriered tape of 1,047,200 in 2007, and lost the record in 2018 when Twin Galaxies' chief Jace Hall showed the tape came off an emulator. The era's ghost story is the Portland cabinet that men in suits are said to have carried away, Polybius.

Later quarters bought more. Sega's Yu Suzuki gave OutRun a Ferrari, a radio and forking roads, and the deluxe cabinet added A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car. Midway's NBA Jam took its burning-hot holler from announcer Tim Kitzrow, and the Tournament Edition hid Bill Clinton in the secret roster. Konami's four-player Simpsons brawler tucked an extra life Behind the bowling alley garbage cans, and its rhythm games wore the brand Bemani. Hollywood paid the favour back: The Last Starfighter rendered its space battles on The Cray X-MP supercomputer, and Wreck-It Ralph seated its villains in a circle chaired by Clyde (the orange ghost).

nintendo-console-games.context_blurb: The Nintendo home-console game lineup from the 1980s through the 2000s was built around the Japanese company's legendary first-party series. Nintendo's first home console was the 1983 Japanese Famicom (Family Computer), re-released in North America in 1985 as the gray Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), which single-handedly saved the American video-game business after the 1983 home-game crash. The NES launched the industry-defining Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda, both led by designer Shigeru Miyamoto, and introduced the lone bounty-hunter sci-fi series Metroid. Nintendo's handheld Game Boy followed in 1989, designed by engineer Gunpei Yokoi, and bundled the Soviet puzzle import Tetris (negotiated by Dutch businessman Henk Rogers). The 16-bit Super Nintendo (SNES) launched in 1991 with Super Mario World and later hosted Squaresoft's Chrono Trigger (1995). The Nintendo 64 arrived in 1996 with Super Mario 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998), Mario Kart 64, Super Smash Bros., and the British studio Rare's GoldenEye 007 and Perfect Dark. Pokemon Red and Blue (1996 Japan, 1998 US) made Game Freak a household name. The GameCube (2001), Wii (2006) with motion controls, and the handheld 3DS and Switch continued the line, with Smash Bros. Melee emerging as a legendary competitive scene.

sega-sony-microsoft-consoles.context_blurb: Nintendo faced rival home game consoles during the industry's 1990s-2000s expansion, each with its own defining games. Sega — the Japanese company that had dominated the arcades — launched the 16-bit Genesis in North America in 1989 under the slogan 'Genesis does what Nintendon't,' adding its new blue-hedgehog mascot Sonic in 1991, the brawler Streets of Rage, and the oddball Earthworm Jim; followed by the troubled 1995 Saturn and the beloved 1998-1999 Dreamcast (famously launched in the US on 9/9/99) with the first fully 3D Sonic Adventure. Sony entered gaming in 1994 with the gray CD-based PlayStation, which launched Capcom's horror classic Resident Evil (1996), Konami's stealth action game Metal Gear Solid (1998), Konami's atmospheric horror Silent Hill (1999), Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996), Final Fantasy VII (1997), and Konami's reinvented exploration-based Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (1997). The follow-up PlayStation 2 (2000) became the bestselling console in history. Microsoft entered the market in 2001 with the chunky black Xbox and its launch title Halo: Combat Evolved from the Seattle studio Bungie. The British studio Core Design's Tomb Raider (1996) also defined this console era. If you are curious about where modern console gaming came from, these three generations of consoles are where almost every signature franchise alive today was first forged.

fighting-games.context_blurb:
The fighting game as everybody knows it starts with Capcom in 1991. Street Fighter II put eight world warriors into one-on-one duels, each with special moves hidden behind joystick motions, and the one everybody learned first belongs to Ryu: hands cupped at the hip, thrown forward, a ball of blue energy, done with a quarter-circle forward and a punch, and it is called the Hadoken. The same game gave the genre its first playable woman, a detective from Chinese Interpol in a blue cheongsam, with hair in ox-horn buns and spikes on her bracelets, whose rapid kick is the Hundred Rending Legs, and she is Chun-Li. Akira Yasuda designed the costume out of Chinese opera.

Midway answered from Chicago in 1992 by filming real actors and digitising them into sprites. Mortal Kombat's selling point was the gruesome finishing move, and the name for it is the Fatality. When a beaten opponent stands swaying, the announcer's two words are Finish him. You then had about five seconds to enter the right sequence. Those Fatalities put the game in front of a United States Senate hearing, which is where the ESRB ratings came from in 1994. Home ports split the difference, since Nintendo's version removed the blood while Sega's hid it behind a six-button code typed at the title screen, and the code was ABACABB. It is a nod to the band Genesis and their 1981 album.

Arcade rumour was half the fun. A green ninja could be fought on the Pit stage in the first Mortal Kombat under conditions nobody could quite confirm, silhouettes crossing the moon and flawless rounds and no blocking, and that character is Reptile. Capcom did the same thing in 1994 in Super Street Fighter II Turbo with a hidden boss, a dark-energy master who is the brother of Ryu and Ken's teacher Gouken, and he is Akuma (Gouki in Japan).

Namco, the Pac-Man studio, took the genre into three dimensions in 1994 with a family feud among the Mishimas, cruel grandfather Heihachi, his son Kazuya and his grandson Jin, plus oddities like the ghost-samurai Yoshimitsu, in a series whose name means iron fist: Tekken. Sega's Virtua Fighter had reached 3D first, in 1993, but the home port made the difference.

One footnote for completists. Disney's Wreck-It Ralph in 2012 put real game villains into a support group, and the studio got permission for the characters but not for every original voice, so one of them had to be dubbed fresh: Kano (Mortal Kombat) — his original arcade-voice was not licensed. If competitive gaming interests you, all of this still runs, every year, at Evo.

king-of-kong-and-arcade-lore.context_blurb: Arcade high-score chasing has legends of its own. The core story is centered on Walter Day's arcade in a small Iowa town, which in the early 1980s became the official Twin Galaxies scorekeeper for every classic arcade cabinet in America. Day tracked player scores, verified records with Polaroids, and built the mythology around the two fiercest Donkey Kong rivals: the Florida pizza-parlor owner Billy Mitchell — who in 1982 posted the Donkey Kong record and later claimed the first-ever perfect Pac-Man score at a Funspot arcade in Weirs Beach, New Hampshire — and the Washington state high-school science teacher Steve Wiebe, who challenged him in 2003 and became famous through the 2007 Seth Gordon documentary The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters. Other legendary arcade lore includes Pac-Man's integer-overflow 'kill screen,' Donkey Kong's kill screen, the 'Minus World' glitch in Super Mario Bros., the Konami Code (dreamed up by Konami programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto), the infamous Alamogordo, New Mexico desert burial of unsold Atari E.T. cartridges, the Polybius urban legend, Ms. Pac-Man's bootleg origin, and arcade cameos in The Last Starfighter (1984), WarGames (1983), Wreck-It Ralph (2012), and Stranger Things. If you want to understand what classic arcade culture felt like, that 2007 documentary is the single best place to start — it captures the whole scene better than any history book.

golden-age-comics.context_blurb: American superhero and newspaper-strip comic books ran from the industry's Golden Age (roughly 1938 to 1950) through the Bronze Age and into the Modern Age; the story here stops at about 2003. The founding titles include Action Comics #1 (June 1938), where creators Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster introduced Superman at DC Comics; Detective Comics #27 (May 1939) where Batman debuted; the 1941 Captain America #1 by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby; the 1941 Wonder Woman by psychologist William Moulton Marston; and the 1961 Marvel Silver Age launched by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby with Fantastic Four #1, soon followed by Spider-Man (Lee and Steve Ditko, 1962), the X-Men (1963), the Hulk, Thor, Daredevil, Black Panther (1966), and Wolverine (1974). The great creator-driven storylines include Chris Claremont's long X-Men run (1975-1991), Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's Watchmen (1986), Frank Miller's Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (1986) and Daredevil run, Neil Gaiman's Sandman (1989-1996), Mike Mignola's Hellboy (1994), Garth Ennis's Preacher and Punisher MAX, Jeff Smith's self-published Bone (1991-2004), Mark Millar's Kick-Ass (2008), and newspaper strips like Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes, Herge's Belgian Tintin, Berkeley Breathed's Bloom County, Hal Foster's Prince Valiant, and Lee Falk's The Phantom.

mcu-through-endgame.context_blurb: The Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) through 2019's Avengers: Endgame is the twenty-three-film interconnected franchise that Marvel Studios produced from 2008 to 2019 under studio head Kevin Feige, now officially designated the Infinity Saga. The story here stops at Endgame; the later multiverse films and series are not covered. The saga begins in 2008 with Jon Favreau's Iron Man, starring Robert Downey Jr. as the billionaire inventor Tony Stark whose kidnap in Afghanistan forces him to build his first armored suit. Phase 1 expanded the slate with four more solo-hero origin films covering the Hulk, the Norse thunder god and his trickster adopted brother, the serum-enhanced World War II soldier, and the first team-up movie directed by Joss Whedon in 2012. Phases 2 and 3 added the space-outlaw team movie (2014), the sorcerer film (2016, directed by Scott Derrickson), the Wakandan king's solo film (2018, directed by Ryan Coogler), Tom Holland's Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), and two Russo-brothers Captain America sequels (2014 Winter Soldier and 2016 Civil War). The whole arc climaxes with the Russos' Avengers: Infinity War (2018), in which the Mad Titan villain assembles the six Infinity Stones, and Avengers: Endgame (2019), in which the surviving heroes stage a time-heist to undo his snap. Be warned: the questions here give away specific character arcs and plot reveals through Endgame.

harry-potter.context_blurb: Harry Potter is a British fantasy series written by J.K. Rowling, consisting of seven novels published from 1997 to 2007 and adapted into eight films from 2001 to 2011. The world of the books is a secret contemporary magical society hidden within modern Britain, in which wizard children receive their acceptance letter at age eleven and travel by scarlet steam engine from Platform 9 3/4 at London's King's Cross Station to a secret boarding school called Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, located somewhere in the Scottish Highlands. The protagonist is a scrawny orphaned boy with a lightning-shaped scar on his forehead — the only person ever to survive the killing curse of the greatest dark wizard of the age — who begins his first year not knowing he is a wizard at all. Across seven years he makes his two best friends (a tall red-haired boy from a huge pure-blood family and a bushy-haired brilliant girl from a non-magical family), is sorted into one of the four student houses, learns the wizarding sport of Quidditch played on flying broomsticks, and gradually confronts the dark wizard's return. The plot of the series has crossed into common knowledge.

pulp-and-fantasy-literature.context_blurb: Classic pulp and fantasy literature from the late 1800s through the mid-1900s is the foundational material that eventually gave the world modern fantasy, horror, science fiction, and the hardboiled detective novel. The tentpole figures: J.R.R. Tolkien, the Oxford philologist and World War I signals officer whose 1937 children's book The Hobbit and 1954-1955 three-volume epic The Lord of the Rings created modern fantasy around a hairy-footed hobbit, a wandering wizard, a dark lord in a shadowy eastern land, and his One Ring forged in a volcanic mountain. The American horror writer H.P. Lovecraft of Providence, Rhode Island, who in his 1920s and 1930s stories for the pulp magazine Weird Tales invented the cosmic-horror tentacled sea-god Cthulhu, the forbidden book Necronomicon, and the coastal New England towns of Arkham and Innsmouth. The Texan writer Robert E. Howard, who in his bedroom in Cross Plains, Texas created the muscular Cimmerian warrior Conan for Weird Tales in 1932 — along with his Puritan swordsman Solomon Kane and his Pictish king Bran Mak Morn — before his 1936 suicide at age thirty. Edgar Allan Poe, who in 1841 invented the detective story with The Murders in the Rue Morgue and whose 1845 poem The Raven became American gothic's defining work. Edgar Rice Burroughs, who created Tarzan (1912) and the Mars warrior John Carter (1912). The crime-fighting pulp heroes of the 1930s magazines and radio. The hardboiled detective writers Dashiell Hammett (The Maltese Falcon, 1930), Raymond Chandler, and Mickey Spillane (Mike Hammer, 1947). The science-fiction grandmasters Isaac Asimov (Foundation), Frank Herbert (Dune, 1965), Ray Bradbury (Fahrenheit 451, 1953), Robert Heinlein (Starship Troopers, Stranger in a Strange Land), Philip K. Dick (whose novels inspired Blade Runner), and Arthur C. Clarke with Stanley Kubrick (2001: A Space Odyssey). Also the sword-and-sorcery writers Fritz Leiber (Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser), Michael Moorcock (Elric of Melnibone), Lord Dunsany, Clark Ashton Smith, and the Arthurian retellings by T.H. White, Mary Stewart, Marion Zimmer Bradley, and Sir Thomas Malory's foundational 1485 Le Morte d'Arthur.

Bigfoot: The Pacific Northwest. Yeti: The Himalayas. Yowie: Australia. Jerry Crew's casts named Bigfoot. Patterson-Gimlin's subject: Patty, clear in Frame 352; Heironimus claimed a horsehide costume, football helmet; Bill Munns measured the film. Nessie swims in Scotland, About 754 feet deep. The Surgeon's Photograph was credited to a Gynecologist, staged by Big-game hunter Marmaduke Wetherell on a Woolworth's toy submarine.

classic-dnd-and-rpgs.context_blurb:
Dungeons & Dragons, 1974, from TSR, founded 1973 by Gary Gygax and his friend Don Kaye, who staked two thousand dollars, dead within months; then TSR Hobbies, Inc. Home: Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, whose 1968 convention punned the Geneva Convention. Co-creator, Minneapolis, Blackmoor: Dave Arneson. Wargame underneath: Chainmail. Gygax invented the brain-eating illithid, the Mind Flayer.

Original classes included the Cleric; Greyhawk added the Thief; Eldritch Wizardry added Psionic combat and the Intellect Devourer. The hardcovers: Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, whose Monster Manual was the first hardcover D&D rulebook. The blue Basic box: edited by J. Eric Holmes. Moldvay and Mentzer followed; five boxes spell BECMI: Basic, Expert, Companion, Master and Immortals. Aaron Allston's 1991 Rules Cyclopedia pulled it together, set in Mystara. Dragon Magazine ran 1976-2007, Sage Advice ran seventeen years under Skip Williams, a 3rd Edition designer, whose engine rolls d20 over a target.

Cheap plastic toys became the feathered Owlbear, the metal-eating Rust Monster and the finned bulette, the landshark. Corridor-filling jelly: Gelatinous Cube. Six-legged tentacled cat: Displacer Beast, from a 1939 story by A.E. Van Vogt. The Beholder debuted in The 1977 Monster Manual, fires Disintegrate from its top stalk, best struck above and behind, outside the sixty-degree anti-magic cone. Soul in a phylactery: Lich. Dark elves: Drow, serving Lolth. From myth: Pegasus, riddling Sphinx, three-bodied Chimera. Two-headed Prince of Demons: Demogorgon. Platinum god of dragons: Bahamut. Hand-and-eye lich, an anagram of Jack Vance: Vecna. Graz'zt's cambion son: Iuz, demigod ruler of the Empire of Iuz.

Gygax's own wizard, on a dozen spells: Mordenkainen of Oerth. Archwizard names are players' characters, anagrammed or reversed; Bigby belonged to Rob Kuntz, his co-DM. Robilar and Mordenkainen reached Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi, under Castle Greyhawk, thirteen named levels plus sub-levels and pockets. The 1983 box: World of Greyhawk Fantasy Game Setting, mapped by Darlene Pekul, credited simply Darlene. The bright, weird house style: Erol Otus, staff 1979-1982. Ousted, Gygax wrote Gord the Rogue, of the City of Greyhawk. The 1985 coup: Lorraine Williams, an heiress holding the Buck Rogers franchise.

Modules: S1 Tomb of Horrors, first of the Special series, its demilich Acererak, whose green devil face is instant disintegration, no save, its skull gems hold trapped souls, freeing his life-drain when touched. White Plume Mountain: Wave, Whelm and Blackrazor. Blank monster lists: B1 In Search of the Unknown. The million-and-a-half-selling pack-in: B2 The Keep on the Borderlands. Dinosaurs: X1 The Isle of Dread. Giants: Steading of the Hill Giant Chief, then the Vault, a thirty-mile cavern under a false sky, ending in Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits. Hommlet's smiling priest serves the Demon Queen of Spiders, Lolth; the late sequel: T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil. Slavers: Slave Pits of the Undercity. Desert pyramid lich: Amun-Re. Ravenloft's vampire: Strahd von Zarovich, designed by Tracy and wife Laura Hickman, its copied trick a tarot draw randomising Strahd's plans. New domains: The Dark Powers. The 2016 rewrite adds Christopher Perkins.

Dragonlance began in 1984, Dragons of Autumn Twilight; the black-robed twin is Raistlin Majere; Krynn's hidden moon is Nuitari; the age ended with the fiery mountain that crashed onto Istar. Drizzt Do'Urden came from R.A. Salvatore; the intended hero had been Wulfgar of the Tribe of the Elk. Scimitars: Twinkle and Icingdeath. Prequel: The Dark Elf Trilogy - Homeland, Exile, Sojourn. Greenwood's Realms shipped as the 1987 Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a grey box, two maps, and the mortal who replaced the dead goddess of magic: Midnight.

Spelljammer's hippo-headed soldiers: the Giff, Napoleonic infantry with hippopotamus heads; helms come from The Arcane, blue-skinned giants. Planescape's silent ruler is The Lady of Pain; Sigil holds tens of thousands of portals. Dark Sun's look came from Brom, its land-killing magic is Defiling, Tyr's Sorcerer-King is Kalak. Birthright's continent: Cerilia.

The 1979 Michigan State disappearance: James Dallas Egbert III, who died August 16, 1980, in Morganton, North Carolina. The 1982 TV film starred Tom Hanks as Robbie Wheeling, in play Pardieu, who climbs the top of the World Trade Center. The 1984 tract: Jack Chick's, of Dark Dungeons fame, where Debbie casts a Mind Bondage spell on her father. The 1983 cartoon: simply Dungeons & Dragons. Elsewhere: Call of Cthulhu runs Basic Roleplaying, a d100 percentile system, by Sandy Petersen, later a Doom and Quake level designer; Glorantha is Greg Stafford's, founder of Chaosium; Traveller kills characters on survival rolls during chargen; Champions runs on The Hero System; Paranoia orders you to Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!

pokemon-franchise.context_blurb: Pokemon is a Japanese multimedia franchise created by a cartoon-loving game designer who grew up catching beetles in the fields around his hometown of Machida, Japan, and brought that childhood obsession to the Nintendo Game Boy handheld console with his small studio Game Freak. The first two paired versions launched in Japan in February 1996 after six years of near-bankrupt development, and the English-language release followed in the U.S. in 1998. The series put the player in the role of a ten-year-old trainer from a small country town who sets out to catch and train small creatures called Pokemon, battling regional Gym Leaders to earn badges and compete at a championship League. The 1997 anime from studio OLM, following the eternally-ten-year-old trainer Ash Ketchum and his small yellow starter Pokemon through the first game region, became one of the most successful anime adaptations ever. The franchise expanded with the Pokemon Trading Card Game (printed in English in 1999 by Wizards of the Coast), sequel games across many new regions over the decades, side games on the Nintendo 64 and later consoles, and a 2016 global mobile augmented-reality smash hit from Niantic. A 2019 live-action Hollywood feature was the franchise's first live-action theatrical entry. The series' specific first-generation lineup — the three starter choices, the gym-badge list, the ghost-type tower, the glitch Pokemon, the lab-cloned legendary — is deep nostalgia canon for anyone who played the original Game Boy cartridges. If you are interested in gaming history, learning how Pokemon almost did not happen is a great story in its own right.

movie-misc-classics.context_blurb: Some of the best-loved films of the 1980s and early 1990s stand on their own. Goodfellas (1990) is Martin Scorsese's fast, funny, frightening gangster film, with Ray Liotta as Henry Hill, a real New York mobster who rose inside the Lucchese crime family and ended up testifying against his friends. Scorsese built it from a true-crime book by the journalist Nicholas Pileggi, who had interviewed Hill at length. The Thing (1982) is John Carpenter's horror film about an Antarctic research crew who dig up a shape-shifting alien that can copy any living creature it touches, so that no man can trust the one beside him. Rob Bottin built its monsters by hand out of rubber, slime and machinery; the film flopped in a summer that belonged to a much friendlier alien, and it is now counted among the greatest horror films ever made. Cocoon (1985) is Ron Howard's gentle science-fiction story about Florida retirees who swim in a pool where aliens have stored mysterious pods and find themselves feeling young again. Howard had grown up on television as a child actor before he turned director, and his elderly cast, led by Don Ameche, stole the film.
